docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Summarizes aggregated results into a user‑facing response using an LLM.
  • Exists to convert structured results into human‑readable output.
  • Sits after EngineAggregatorNode at the end of the control graph.
  • Class: AnswerSynthesizerNode
  • Source: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/answer_synthesizer/node.py

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Send the model a preview of each result, never the whole of it: the first settings.results.preview_rows rows (20), the total row count, the column names and a partial flag.
  • Say when a result was cut at the row limit, whatever the model wrote.
  • Include unmapped sub‑queries in the response context.
  • Invoke LLM with structured output schema.

docs.title: Position in Execution Graph
docs.text:
Upstream: - EngineAggregatorNode, after a generated run or a verified one (the curated matcher ran the query)

Downstream: - Graph end.

Trigger conditions: - Executed after aggregation succeeds. When the aggregator fails (AGGREGATOR_FAILED), aggregator_route ends the run instead, so this node never spends a model call on an empty result.

flowchart LR
    Aggregator[EngineAggregatorNode] --> Synthesizer[AnswerSynthesizerNode] --> EndNode[PipelineEnd]

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
From GraphState:

  • user_query (required)
  • aggregator_response.terminal_results (required): the first rows of each terminal result
  • aggregator_response.computed_artifacts: the saved result behind each, for its row count and columns
  • decomposer_response.unmapped_subqueries (optional)
  • subgraph_outputs[<id>].truncated / .row_cap: whether a sub-query's result reached its row limit, and at how many rows.
  • verified_match (optional): set when a verified query answered. Its qualified id and its description (the data team's words for what the query returns, e.g. "invoiced revenue, before refunds") are added to the prompt as a Verified Query section, and the model is told to describe the numbers that way. A generated answer's prompt has no such section and is exactly what it was.
  • warnings: the VALUE_NOT_FOUND warnings ("There is no Genre with Name 'Polka'.") from sub-queries whose filter named a value that does not exist (see ExecutorNode). An ERROR-severity one is not used: a retry replaced that attempt.

Validation performed:

  • If no aggregated result is available, emits INVALID_STATE.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Mutations to GraphState:

  • answer_synthesizer_response (AnswerSynthesizerResponse): final_answer is the model's AggregatedResponse (summary, format_type, content, warnings) plus truncated, True when a result was cut at the row limit.
  • reasoning summary
  • errors on failure

Side effects:

  • LLM invocation.

docs.title: Internal Flow (Step-by-Step)
docs.text:
1. Resolve aggregated result from aggregator_response.
  2. If missing, emit INVALID_STATE error and stop.
  3. Build the result preview (result_preview()): for each terminal result, its first settings.results.preview_rows rows, row_count, columns and partial (true when rows were left out). The rows are the aggregator's terminal_results, already cut to the preview; row_count and columns come from the saved combined result in computed_artifacts, so they describe the whole result. Serialize it to JSON.
  4. Build the Result Limit note: one line per sub-query whose result reached its row limit ("The result was cut at 10,000 rows, the row limit, so it is incomplete. Narrow the question ..."), or None.
  5. Serialize unmapped sub‑queries to JSON.
  6. Invoke LLM chain with structured output. The prompt's Data Notes lists the missing values and asks the answer to say the value does not exist instead of reporting the empty result as a finding. When the run was started by stream_query (configurable.stream_answer), the chain is streaming_structured: the same request with the provider asked to stream, so the run's RunEvents callback turns each piece of the tool call into an answer_delta event. The answer it returns is the unstreamed chain's (Streaming a run).
  7. Append each missing-value note and each result-limit note to the answer's warnings, whatever the model wrote, set final_answer.truncated, and return AnswerSynthesizerResponse.
  8. On exception, emit AGGREGATOR_FAILED.

docs.title: The model sees a preview, not the result
docs.text:
The user sees the full result as a table; the model's job is to write about it, not to copy it. So the prompt carries a preview, and its instructions say:

  • every number the answer states comes from the preview rows or from row_count;
  • when the preview is partial, do not total, average, rank or count over rows it cannot see;
  • do not reproduce the result: say the full result is in the table, and use format_type "table" only for a few preview rows.

The prompt's size no longer grows with the result, which is what let the row cap rise from 1,000 to a resource ceiling (settings.results.row_limit, 100,000).

docs.title: A result cut at the row limit
docs.text: The generator bounds each sub-query's SQL at its row limit. A result that comes back with that many rows may have been cut, so the subgraph wrapper marks it truncated (SubgraphOutput, QueryResult.sub_queries[].truncated, QueryResult.truncated). The prompt's Result Limit section tells the model the result was cut at N rows and asks it to say so and to suggest narrowing the question; the node adds the same note to warnings itself, so a cut result is never presented as complete even when the model leaves it out. A plan's own top-N (LIMIT 5) is the answer, not a cut, and is never flagged.

docs.title: Contracts & Interfaces
docs.text:
Implements a LangGraph node callable:

def __call__(self, state: GraphState) -> Dict[str, Any]

Key contracts:

  • AggregatedResponse
  • AnswerSynthesizerResponse

docs.title: Determinism Guarantees
docs.text: • Non‑deterministic unless LLM configured deterministically.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Emits PipelineError with:

  • INVALID_STATE (no aggregated result)
  • AGGREGATOR_FAILED (LLM failure), or a PROVIDER_* error when the provider refused the call (see provider failures)

Logs failures via logger.error.

docs.title: Retry + Idempotency
docs.text:
• No internal retry logic.
  • Idempotency depends on LLM determinism.

docs.title: Performance Characteristics
docs.text:
• LLM call dominates latency and cost.
  • The prompt holds at most settings.results.preview_rows rows per terminal result, whatever the result's size. The whole result is still held in memory by the aggregator.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
• Logger: answer_synthesizer
  • Adds reasoning summary to state.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
• LLM configuration for agent name answer_synthesizer via llm.yaml.
  • settings.results.preview_rows (default 20): rows of each result the model sees.
  • settings.results.row_limit (default 100000): the row ceiling a result is cut at; see the system settings.
  • Both are read from the engine's runtime (ctx.settings) when the node is built, so two engines in one process each use their own.

docs.title: Extension Points
docs.text:
• Modify ANSWER_SYNTHESIZER_PROMPT.
  • Replace node in build_graph() for custom synthesis.

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
• No deterministic summarization guarantees without LLM configuration.
  • No fallback response when LLM fails.

docs.title: Related Code
docs.text: • packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/answer_synthesizer/node.py

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Generates a structured SQL AST plan (PlanModel) using an LLM with structured output.
  • Exists to translate natural language intent into a deterministic, machine‑verifiable plan.
  • Sits after SchemaRetrieverNode in the SQL agent subgraph.
  • Class: ASTPlannerNode
  • Source: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/ast_planner/node.py

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Serve a pinned plan from the plan cache on a first attempt, without an LLM call.
  • Serialize relevant_tables into the planning prompt.
  • Pass user intent, expected schema, and error feedback to the LLM.
  • Return ASTPlannerResponse with the PlanModel and its plan_source ("llm" or "cache").

docs.title: Position in Execution Graph
docs.text:
Upstream: - SchemaRetrieverNode - RefinerNode (retry loop)

Downstream: - LogicalValidatorNode on success - retry_handler on retryable failure

Trigger conditions: - Executed after schema retrieval and during retry loops.

flowchart LR
    SchemaRetriever[SchemaRetrieverNode] --> Planner[ASTPlannerNode] --> Validator[LogicalValidatorNode]
    Refiner[RefinerNode] --> Planner
    Planner --> RetryHandler[retry_handler]

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
From SubgraphExecutionState:

  • sub_query.intent (required)
  • sub_query.expected_schema (optional)
  • sub_query.metrics, filters, group_by, order_by, limit: rendered by semantic_context_of() as compact JSON into [SEMANTIC_CONTEXT] (empty when the sub-query has none). The system message tells the model to apply all of it, filters on a metric as having, order_by as the plan's order_by and limit as the plan's limit, and that a most/least/top-N question needs an order_by on the ranked value and a limit; one example shows it.
  • relevant_tables (required for schema grounding)
  • errors (optional feedback for retries)

Validation performed:

  • No explicit validation; relies on LLM structured output schema.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Mutations to SubgraphExecutionState:

  • ast_planner_response (ASTPlannerResponse)
  • reasoning with plan summary
  • errors on planning failure

Side effects:

  • LLM invocation via llm_registry (none on a plan cache hit).
  • Reads the plan cache in the schema store. It never writes it: the sub-query wrapper stores a plan only after it validated and executed.

docs.title: Plan cache
docs.text:
The planner is the call that decides the SQL, so a plan that already passed validation and executed is reused (pipeline/plan_cache.py).

  • Key: (normalised sub_query.intent, sub_query.datasource_id, sub_query.schema_version). When the sub-query has an order_by or limit, they are appended to the intent part (... | order_by=album_count desc | limit=1), so a top-1 and a top-5 of the same intent are different entries. The run date is always appended (... | today=2026-10-12): the planner is told today's date and writes relative dates as literals, so a plan from another day misses. Normalisation case-folds, collapses whitespace and strips trailing .?!,;:; the match is exact. No schema_version, no caching.
  • Read: only on a first attempt (retry_count == 0 and no errors). A hit returns ASTPlannerResponse(plan=<cached>, plan_source="cache") and makes no LLM call; a retry after a rejected plan always asks the model.
  • Never trusted: the logical validator, generator and executor run on a cached plan exactly as on a fresh one, so RBAC and policy changes apply.
  • Written by wrap_subgraph (pipeline/graph_utils.py) only when the sub-query produced SQL and executed without a blocking error. Refused, failed and plan-only runs are not stored.
  • Controls: settings.pipeline.plan_cache (default true) and nl2sql cache clear.

See Determinism → The plan cache.

docs.title: Internal Flow (Step-by-Step)
docs.text:
1. On a first attempt, look up the plan cache; on a hit, return the cached plan with plan_source="cache" and stop.
  2. Render relevant_tables with render_schema_for_prompt (see below).
  3. Build the feedback string from the latest attempt's errors only, one JSON object per line with node, error_code and message (nl2sql.pipeline.retry_feedback): an earlier attempt's errors, stack traces and details are never sent.
  4. Build expected_schema payload from sub‑query.
  5. Invoke the LLM chain with prompt + structured output (PlanModel).
  6. Return ASTPlannerResponse with plan and reasoning.
  7. On exception, emit PLANNING_FAILURE error and return plan=None.

docs.title: Prompt layout and caching
docs.text:
The prompt is two messages, so providers can cache the stable part (OpenAI caches a stable prefix of 1,024+ tokens automatically):

Message Content Changes system (PLANNER_SYSTEM_PROMPT) role, instructions, output contract, constraints, PLANNER_EXAMPLES, then [RELEVANT_TABLES] only when the schema or the caller's role changes human (PLANNER_HUMAN_PROMPT) [TODAY], [EXPECTED_SCHEMA], [SEMANTIC_CONTEXT], [FEEDBACK], [USER_QUERY] every call

[TODAY] is the run date (run_date(today) in common/dates.py, given settings.pipeline.today: that date when it is set, else the UTC date), so "this year" or "the last 30 days" resolve to real dates rather than a year the model guessed. It is in the human message because it changes daily; in the system message it would invalidate the cached prefix every midnight. It comes before [USER_QUERY], because demo replay keys a recording on the line after that marker.

The examples come before the schema so that the instructions and examples (about 1,300 tokens) stay cacheable even when vector retrieval picks a different set of tables per question. The system/human boundary is the single cache seam: keep per-question content out of the system message.

The schema block (render_schema_for_prompt in schema_retriever/schema.py) is one compact JSON object per table, tables sorted by name (a datasource's preferred tables first, each with "preferred":true) and keys sorted, so the same snapshot and role render byte-identically. Instruction 14 tells the model to plan against a preferred table when it answers the question; see preferred tables. It drops empty fields and schema_version. Of the column statistics only sample_values is sent (it helps match literal filters such as 'Rock' or 'USA'), plus range, [min_value, max_value], for a date, time or numeric column that is not a key. For a text column with at most 50 distinct values sample_values is every value, so "heavy metal" can be matched to 'Heavy Metal'; for a larger one it is the five most frequent (ALL_VALUES_MAX_DISTINCT in adapters/sqlalchemy_base/adapter.py). A date kept as text (every date in SQLite; opened_at in the support demo) is recognised by its ISO values and gets a range instead of sample_values. The range is what lets instruction 13 work: when "this year" or "the last 30 days" falls outside a date column's range, the planner uses the latest such period in the data and says so in its reasoning, rather than planning a filter that is certain to return nothing. null_percentage and distinct_count stay in the snapshot. On Chinook the ranges cost about 140 tokens of schema block (2,324 to 2,466).

Measured on Chinook with tiktoken o200k_base, its 12 demo questions, no LLM call (python scripts/measure_prompt_tokens.py):

before after planner prompt 8,921 tokens 3,495 tokens schema block 7,754 tokens 2,324 tokens prefix identical across questions 8,122 tokens 3,460 tokens

docs.title: Contracts & Interfaces
docs.text:
Implements a LangGraph node callable:

def __call__(self, state: SubgraphExecutionState) -> Dict[str, Any]

Key contracts:

  • PlanModel
  • ASTPlannerResponse

DISTINCT in the plan language: PlanModel.distinct: true is SELECT DISTINCT, and a func expr with distinct: true is a distinct aggregate such as COUNT(DISTINCT x). The system message's instructions and one of its examples say so; a function named DISTINCT is rejected by the logical validator.

Dates in the plan language are two portable functions, described once in the system message and the same for every database: DATE_PART(unit, date), an integer, and DATE_TRUNC(unit, date), the period's first day as YYYY-MM-DD, with the unit a string literal year, quarter, month or day. The prompt names no database; each adapter renders the functions (see the generator). Subqueries and window functions are not in the language. offset pages through the plan's order_by (rows 11 to 20 are limit: 10, offset: 10); a plan with an offset and no order_by is rejected by the validator.

docs.title: Determinism Guarantees
docs.text:
• Deterministic only if LLM is configured deterministically.
  • Plan structure is validated downstream; ordering is not enforced here.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Emits PipelineError with:

  • PLANNING_FAILURE on LLM or parsing errors; a provider's refusal of the call is a PROVIDER_* error instead (see provider failures).

Logs failures via logger.exception.

docs.title: Retry + Idempotency
docs.text:
• Retries are orchestrated by the subgraph, not this node.
  • Idempotency depends on LLM determinism.

docs.title: Performance Characteristics
docs.text:
• One LLM call per planning attempt.
  • Cost is dominated by LLM latency and token usage.

docs.title: Observability

  • Adds reasoning entries to subgraph state.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Answers a question with a verified query from curated.yaml when one fits, before the model plans anything.
  • Searches only the verified queries of datasources the caller's role may read, asks the model once to pick one and give its parameter values, and checks the values and the role's table access in code.
  • Runs the saved SQL with the values as bound parameters, under the row ceiling, and hands the result to the aggregator and the answer synthesizer as a one-sub-query run.
  • Falls back to the generated pipeline for anything else, with a reason code; a fallback is never an error of the run.
  • Class: CuratedMatcherNode
  • Source: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/curated_matcher/node.py
  • Design: Curated answers

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Limit the search to datasources that have verified queries and that rbac.get_allowed_datasources() allows (the pinned datasource_id only, when one is given).
  • Retrieve candidates with VectorStore.retrieve_verified_query_candidates() (top settings.curated.match_top_k), skipping a query that is in the index but no longer in the file.
  • Ask no model when the best similarity is below settings.curated.match_floor.
  • Make one structured-output call, VerifiedQueryChoice.
  • Check the chosen values (params.resolve_params): type, min/max, choices, required.
  • Check every table the SQL reads against the role's allowed_tables with table_allowed(), and that the SQL is still one read-only query.
  • Check the adapter declares SUPPORTS_BOUND_PARAMETERS before running a query with parameters.
  • Run the SQL through SqlExecutorService with ExecutorRequest.parameters and max_rows.
  • On a hit, fill the state the way a one-sub-query generated run leaves it.

docs.title: Position in Execution Graph
docs.text:
The node is in the graph only when curated answers are on: CURATED_ENABLED is true, the curated file is loaded and holds at least one verified query, and the run executes (a plan-only run has no matcher). Otherwise the graph starts at DatasourceResolverNode, exactly as without curated answers.

Upstream: - Entry point (no upstream nodes).

Downstream: - layer_router on a hit: the scan is already done, so it sends the run to EngineAggregatorNode, then AnswerSynthesizerNode. - DatasourceResolverNode on any fallback.

flowchart LR
    Matcher[CuratedMatcherNode] -->|verified| Router[layer_router]
    Router --> Aggregator[EngineAggregatorNode]
    Aggregator --> Synth[AnswerSynthesizerNode]
    Matcher -->|fallback| Resolver[DatasourceResolverNode]

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
From GraphState:

  • user_query (str, required): searched, and shown to the model.
  • datasource_id (Optional[str]): when set, only this datasource is searched.
  • user_context (UserContext, required): the role's datasources and tables.

Context dependencies (Runtime):

  • curated: the loaded CuratedFileConfig. The matcher reads every query from it, never from the index.
  • vector_store: retrieve_verified_query_candidates().
  • rbac: get_allowed_datasources() and get_allowed_tables().
  • ds_registry: dialect, adapter row limit, supports().
  • schema_store: the latest schema version, stamped on the sub-query.
  • llm_registry: the choice's model, agent name curatedmatcher (falls back to default).

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
On a hit, mutations to GraphState:

  • verified_match (VerifiedMatch: datasource_id, query_id, description, params)
  • decomposer_response: one SubQuery (id verified_<query_id>, intent the question) in one standalone combine group
  • execution_dag: build_execution_dag() of that response
  • artifact_refs: the saved result
  • subgraph_outputs: one SubgraphOutput with plan_source="verified", the SQL, row_cap, truncated, and the checks read_only, params and policy
  • reasoning

On a fallback: nothing the rest of the graph reads. execution_failed also adds a warnings entry.

Always, outside the state (the trace keeps the node's whole return):

  • curated_match: matched, reason (a fallback code or None), detail, floor, candidates (datasource_id, query_id, similarity), choice (the model's query_id, params, reason), params (after checking).
  • retrieval: the search's record, shaped like the resolver's, when a search ran.

docs.title: Internal Flow (Step-by-Step)
docs.text:
1. Searchable datasources: registered, allowed for the role (* allows all), the pinned one alone if pinned, and holding verified queries. None: not_configured, no search and no embedding call.
  2. Candidates. None (or none still in the file): no_candidates.
  3. Best similarity below settings.curated.match_floor: below_floor, no model call.
  4. One VerifiedQueryChoice call. It raised (no recording in a replay, a provider error): model_failed. none_of_these: none_of_these. An id that is not a candidate: unknown_query.
  5. Values: an unknown name, a name twice, a value that does not parse or is out of bounds: param_invalid; a param with no default left out or empty: param_missing. A param left out takes its default.
  6. Tables: any table the SQL reads not allowed for the role: policy_denied. The normal pipeline then enforces RBAC as always; the user is not told a verified query exists.
  7. Capability: a query with params on an adapter without SUPPORTS_BOUND_PARAMETERS: capability_missing.
  8. Run with the values bound and max_rows set to min(adapter.row_limit or row_limit, row_limit) (row_limit is settings.results.row_limit). Failed or no result: execution_failed, with a warning.
  9. Fill the state and route to layer_router.

docs.title: The choice prompt
docs.text:
System message (curated_matcher/prompts.py), then the question after a User Query: line, which nl2sql.llm.replay.extract_question recognises:

You decide whether one of the verified queries below answers the user's question. A data team wrote and checked each one; you cannot change what a query does, only pick one and give its parameter values.

Rules:
1. Pick a query only when it answers the whole question as asked: the same measure, the same ranking or grouping, the same filters. A query about something close but different (ranked by another measure, grouped another way, a different entity) does not answer it.
2. When no query answers the whole question, set query_id to "none_of_these". When unsure, choose "none_of_these": the question is then answered another way, which is better than a wrong answer.
3. Use the id exactly as listed (datasource.query).
4. Give a value for each parameter the question states, as text: an int as digits, a date as YYYY-MM-DD, a string exactly as one of its choices when it has them. Leave out a parameter the question does not state; never guess a value the question does not give.
5. Give the reason in one short sentence.

Verified queries (JSON):
{candidates}

{candidates} lists, in ranked order, each candidate's qualified id (chinook.top_customers_by_revenue), its description, and its params with type, bounds, choices, default and required. Never the SQL.

docs.title: Contracts & Interfaces
docs.text:
def __call__(self, state: GraphState) -> Dict[str, Any]

Key contracts:

  • VerifiedQueryChoice, ParamValue, VerifiedMatch (curated_matcher/schemas.py)
  • VerifiedQueryCandidate (indexing/models.py)
  • ExecutorRequest.parameters, ExecutorRequest.max_rows
  • SubgraphOutput with plan_source="verified"

docs.title: Determinism Guarantees
docs.text:
• No model writes or edits the SQL; the model picks an id and supplies values, which code checks and the driver binds.
  • The candidates block is serialized with sorted keys in ranked order.
  • The search and the choice are as deterministic as the embedding model and the configured temperature and seed.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text: The node never adds an error to the run. Every failure, including an unexpected exception, is a fallback with a reason code: not_configured, no_candidates, below_floor, none_of_these, model_failed, unknown_query, param_invalid, param_missing, policy_denied, capability_missing, execution_failed.

docs.title: Retry + Idempotency
docs.text:
• No retry: a fallback runs the generated pipeline instead.
  • Idempotent for the same input state and the same model answer.

docs.title: Performance Characteristics
docs.text:
• A verified answer costs two model calls (this choice and the answer) instead of four or more.
  • Below the floor, or with no candidates, a fallback costs one embedding call and no model call.
  • The result is read in batches and the stream stops at max_rows.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
• Logger: curated_matcher
  • The trace records the node with its curated_match record and the search; the choice call is recorded like every LLM call, under node curated_matcher.
  • QueryResult.source says verified with the query id and values, or generated.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Picks the datasources a question goes to: an explicit override, the only registered datasource, or a vector search when more than one is registered.
  • Enforces RBAC and the schema version mismatch policy before planning.
  • Refuses a question no datasource can answer, with one small structured LLM call, before the decomposer runs.
  • Sits at the entry of the control graph and gates the pipeline.
  • Class: DatasourceResolverNode
  • Source: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/datasource_resolver/node.py

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Choose candidate datasources:
    • an explicit datasource_id is used as given;
    • with exactly one datasource registered, that one is used and no vector search runs;
    • otherwise VectorStore.retrieve_datasource_candidates() ranks them.
  • Validate datasource IDs against the registered adapter list.
  • Enforce RBAC datasource access.
  • Detect schema version mismatches and apply the configured policy.
  • Judge answerability over the allowed candidates, refuse with QUESTION_NOT_ANSWERABLE when none can answer, and forward only the candidates the verdict names.
  • Give each forwarded datasource its description and a capped table list, for the decomposer to route on.
  • Populate DatasourceResolverResponse in GraphState.

docs.title: Position in Execution Graph
docs.text:
Upstream: - Entry point (no upstream nodes), or CuratedMatcherNode when curated answers are configured and it fell back.

Downstream: - DecomposerNode if resolution succeeds. - Terminates early (END) if no datasource is allowed, or the question is not answerable.

Trigger conditions: - The control graph's entry node, unless curated answers are configured; then it runs whenever the curated matcher did not answer.

flowchart LR
    Resolver[DatasourceResolverNode] -->|answerable and allowed| Decomposer[DecomposerNode]
    Resolver -->|denied or not answerable| EndNode[END]

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
From GraphState:

  • user_query (str, required): the question; used for vector retrieval (more than one datasource) and for the answerability check.
  • datasource_id (Optional[str]): explicit override for datasource selection.
  • user_context (UserContext, required): RBAC enforcement.

Context dependencies (Runtime):

  • vector_store: needed only when more than one datasource is registered and no override is given; missing then, the resolver returns SCHEMA_RETRIEVAL_FAILED.
  • ds_registry: adapter registry for registered IDs.
  • schema_store: latest schema versions, and the latest snapshot's description and table list for the answerability check and the decomposer's routing context.
  • rbac: filters allowed datasources.
  • llm_registry: the answerability check's model, agent name datasourceresolver (falls back to default).

Validation performed:

  • Datasource override must exist in the registry.
  • RBAC must allow at least one candidate.
  • Version mismatch policy enforced via settings.schema.version_mismatch.
  • At least one allowed candidate must be judged able to answer.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Mutations to GraphState:

  • datasource_resolver_response (DatasourceResolverResponse)
  • errors (list of PipelineError) on failure
  • reasoning (how the candidates were chosen, and the answerability reason) and warnings

Side effects:

  • One LLM call (the answerability check) once the role check passes.
  • A vector store retrieval when more than one datasource is registered and no override is given.

docs.title: Internal Flow (Step-by-Step)
docs.text:
1. Candidates:
    • state.datasource_id set: it must be registered (INVALID_STATE otherwise); it is the only candidate.
    • Exactly one datasource registered: it is the only candidate; no vector search.
    • Otherwise: the vector store must exist (SCHEMA_RETRIEVAL_FAILED otherwise); retrieve_datasource_candidates(k=5) gives the candidates (an exact ranking of every datasource entry, so no datasource is missed by the approximate search), and none is SCHEMA_RETRIEVAL_FAILED (with a re-index hint when the index is empty).
  2. Role check: candidates the role may not read are dropped. None left is a CRITICAL SECURITY_VIOLATION, and no model call is made.
  3. Schema version mismatch policy (fail returns INVALID_STATE; warn adds a warning).
  4. Answerability check over the allowed candidates only (see below). An empty verdict returns QUESTION_NOT_ANSWERABLE.
  5. Narrow to the verdict. After a vector search, only the allowed candidates the verdict names go forward; a candidate the verdict rejects never reaches the decomposer, and a verdict naming only unknown ids is QUESTION_NOT_ANSWERABLE. With an override or a single datasource there is one candidate, and a non-empty verdict accepts it.
  6. Attach routing context to each forwarded datasource, from the latest schema snapshot: description, tables (sorted bare table names, at most 30) and more_tables (how many were left out).
  7. Return DatasourceResolverResponse with the forwarded datasources (sorted by id), their IDs as allowed_datasource_ids, and unsupported IDs.
  8. On exceptions, log and return SCHEMA_RETRIEVAL_FAILED with the exception text; a provider's refusal of the model call is a PROVIDER_* error instead (see provider failures).

A single registered datasource is the shortcut, not the usual case: with more than one - the demo registers three - the vector search runs, and nothing else in the flow changes.

docs.title: Order of checks
docs.text:
The role check runs before the answerability check, so:

  • a caller with no allowed datasource gets the RBAC refusal and the model is never asked;
  • the model sees only datasources the role may read;
  • a question that is answerable but touches tables the role may not read passes this node and is refused by LogicalValidatorNode's table policy, as before.

docs.title: Answerability check
docs.text:
A structured call (AnswerabilityResponse: answerable_datasource_ids, reason) with this prompt (datasource_resolver/prompts.py). The system message:

You check whether a question can be answered from the datasources below, before any SQL is planned. For each datasource you see its description and the tables it holds, not its data.

Rules:
1. List the id of every datasource that could hold data relevant to the question, even partly. A question that needs several datasources lists all of them.
2. Be conservative. When you are unsure, treat the question as answerable and list the datasources that might answer it. Refusing a question that could have been answered is worse than running one that finds nothing.
3. Return an empty list only when the question is clearly about something none of these datasources hold, such as the weather, general knowledge, or small talk.
4. Use only ids from the list below.
5. Give the reason in one short sentence.

Datasources (JSON):
{datasources}

The human message:

User Query:
{user_query}
  • {datasources} is a JSON list, one entry per allowed candidate, sorted by id, with sorted keys: description (the datasource description from the latest schema snapshot, which indexing takes from the datasources config) and tables (sorted bare table names).
  • The instructions and datasources come first (the system message) and the question last (the human message), so the prompt is byte-identical across questions up to the question and a provider's prompt cache can serve the prefix. OpenAI caches only prompts of 1,024 tokens or more, so with one small datasource nothing is cached; the prefix grows, and becomes cacheable, with more datasources.
  • The verdict refuses and narrows: an empty list refuses the question, and after a vector search only the allowed candidates it names reach the decomposer. It cannot add a datasource the role may not read.
  • For Chinook on its own the rendered prompt is about 260 tokens (o200k_base), plus the AnswerabilityResponse function schema; the demo now registers three datasources, so its prompt is correspondingly longer.

docs.title: Contracts & Interfaces
docs.text:
Implements a LangGraph node callable:

def __call__(self, state: GraphState) -> Dict[str, Any]

Key contracts:

  • DatasourceResolverResponse
  • ResolvedDatasource
  • AnswerabilityResponse
  • PipelineError

docs.title: Determinism Guarantees
docs.text:
• Candidate choice is deterministic for an override or a single datasource.
  • Vector ranking may vary with more than one datasource.
  • The answerability prompt is serialized deterministically; the verdict is a model call at the configured temperature and seed.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Emits PipelineError with:

  • INVALID_STATE (unknown datasource override; schema version mismatch under fail)
  • SECURITY_VIOLATION (RBAC denial)
  • QUESTION_NOT_ANSWERABLE (ERROR: no allowed datasource can answer the question; QueryResult.status is error)
  • SCHEMA_RETRIEVAL_FAILED (no candidates, no vector store with several datasources, or exceptions)

Exceptions are caught at the node boundary and logged with logger.error.

docs.title: Retry + Idempotency
docs.text:
• No internal retry logic.
  • Idempotent for the same input state, except vector retrieval ranking and the model's verdict may vary.

docs.title: Performance Characteristics
docs.text:
• One small LLM call per question once the role check passes; it saves the decomposer, planner and synthesizer calls on every unanswerable question.
  • A vector store retrieval (MMR search) only with more than one datasource.
  • RBAC checks are in-memory operations; schema lookups are store reads.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
• Logger: datasource_resolver
  • The answerability call is recorded like every LLM call: usage under node datasource_resolver in QueryResult.usage, and in the run trace keyed by node, sub-query, attempt and call.
  • Vector retrieval uses VECTOR_BREAKER at the vector store layer.
  • Returns a retrieval record in its update for the run trace: the query embedded and the datasource search's pool with scores, MMR picks and drops; or skipped: true and why (an explicit datasource_id, a single registered datasource, no vector store). The answerability check is not part of it: it is an LLM call and is traced as one. See Debugging a run.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
• settings.schema.version_mismatch (warn, fail or ignore)
  • LLM agent datasourceresolver in the LLM config (optional; see LLM configuration)

docs.title: Extension Points
docs.text:
• Replace this node in build_graph() to change resolution behavior.
  • Extend retrieval by modifying the node or the vector store retrieval strategy.

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
• Tenant scoping is not implemented in vector retrieval.
  • The answerability check sees table names, not columns or data, so it refuses only questions clearly outside every datasource.

docs.title: Related Code
docs.text:
• packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/datasource_resolver/node.py
  • packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/datasource_resolver/prompts.py
  • packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/datasource_resolver/schemas.py

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Decomposes the user query into datasource‑scoped sub‑queries and combination operations.
  • Produces deterministic IDs for sub‑queries and post‑combine ops.
  • Sits after DatasourceResolverNode and before the layer router.
  • Class: DecomposerNode
  • Source: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/decomposer/node.py

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Invoke the LLM to produce DecomposerResponse.
  • Filter sub‑queries by resolved/allowed/unsupported datasources.
  • Stabilize IDs using a hash of sub‑query content.
  • Normalize and sort combine groups and post‑combine operations.
  • Build the ExecutionDAG the layer router walks and the aggregator runs (decomposer/dag.py). The DAG is a pure function of the response above, so it is code here rather than a node of its own.

docs.title: Position in Execution Graph
docs.text:
Upstream: - DatasourceResolverNode

Downstream: - layer_router

Trigger conditions: - Executed only when resolver_route returns continue.

flowchart LR
    Resolver[DatasourceResolverNode] --> Decomposer[DecomposerNode] --> Router[layer_router]

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
From GraphState:

  • user_query (str, required)
  • datasource_resolver_response (DatasourceResolverResponse, required)

Validation performed:

  • Raises if no resolved datasources are available.
  • Filters out sub‑queries that reference missing, restricted, or unsupported datasources.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Mutations to GraphState:

  • decomposer_response (DecomposerResponse)
  • reasoning (completion status)
  • errors on failure

Side effects:

  • None beyond LLM invocation.

docs.title: Internal Flow (Step-by-Step)
docs.text:
1. Validate resolver response; raise if no resolved datasources.
  2. Build resolved_payload and schema_version_map. The payload has one entry per resolved datasource, sorted by id: datasource_id, description, tables (sorted bare table names, at most 30, set by the resolver) and more_tables (how many tables were left out, present only when some were). The resolver fills these for every path, so an explicit datasource_id or a single registered datasource gets the same context as a vector search. The index metadata (chunk id, type, schema version) is not sent.
  3. Invoke LLM chain with user_query and resolved datasources. The prompt is two messages: the system message holds the fixed instructions and output format (cacheable), the human message holds the resolved datasources (as JSON with sorted keys) and then the question. Rule 1 tells the model to pick each sub-query's datasource from these descriptions and tables. A sub-query carries its own filters (a threshold on a metric included), order_by and limit: "the artist with the most albums" is order_by album_count desc, limit 1. post_combine_ops are only for operations across two or more combined sub-queries, and the prompt's example has none. The answer is a call to the DecomposerResponse tool whose arguments are the decomposition itself; both the prompt and the tool's description (the model's docstring) say not to wrap them under another key, which Claude did on the anthropic wire while the tool had no description.
  4. fold_single_input_ops() then moves every filter, sort and limit op on a combine group with one sub-query (used by no other group) into that sub-query: filters are appended, order_by terms appended, and the smallest limit kept. With one input there is nothing to combine, and left as post-combine ops they reached only the aggregated answer, never the sub-query's SQL or rows (the first gpt-5.4 tier 2 run returned every row for ten superlative and top-N questions this way). A group with an aggregate or project op is left to the aggregator.
  5. For each LLM sub‑query:
  6. Validate datasource existence and RBAC allowance.
  7. Assign deterministic ID via _stable_id(), over the intent, metrics, filters, group_by, order_by, limit and expected schema.
  8. Two sub-queries the model wrote identically hash to the same ID, but each is still a sub-query of its own (a combine group may name both), so a repeat takes the next ordinal: sq_<hash>, sq_<hash>_2, and so on. Both run, and the DAG gets one scan node per sub-query. Before this, the shared ID gave the DAG one node id for two nodes, and the run ended with PLANNER_FAILED ("contains a cycle").
  9. Attach schema version.
  10. Remap combine groups to stable sub‑query IDs. An input whose sub-query was dropped in step 4 is removed from its group, and a group left with no inputs is removed. A join or compare group left with fewer than two inputs is refused: the run ends here with PLANNER_FAILED, before any scan runs, and no DAG is built. The message names the group and why each input was dropped (restricted_datasource, no_datasource, unsupported_datasource) but not the datasource. The model is not asked again: a restricted or unresolved datasource is not something a new decomposition changes. Before this, the group was kept with its one input and the engine returned that side alone as the "join", so "customers with an open ticket who spent the most" was answered as "customers who spent the most", with no error. A union that lost an input still runs on the inputs that remain; the dropped intent is reported in unmapped_subqueries.
  11. Assign deterministic IDs to post‑combine ops.
  12. Sort sub‑queries, combine groups, and post‑combine ops.
  13. Check every post-combine op against the columns its combine group will produce (post_combine_problems()). A sub-query's result columns are its expected_schema names (the logical validator holds each plan to them), and the combined columns follow by the engine's own rules in nl2sql/aggregation/columns.py: a join/compare drops the right-hand join keys and suffixes any other right-hand name the left also has with _right. A group whose sub-query declares no expected_schema is not checked. If an op reads a column that will not exist, the model is asked once more, with the reason appended to the human message ("PREVIOUS ANSWER REJECTED: ..."). A second rejected answer ends the run here with PLANNER_FAILED and the same reason, before any scan runs; nothing after the decomposer can ask for a new decomposition, so this used to fail in the aggregator after every scan.
  14. Return DecomposerResponse.
  15. On exception, emit ORCHESTRATOR_CRASH error.

docs.text:

def __call__(self, state: GraphState) -> Dict[str, Any]

Key contracts:

  • DecomposerResponse
  • SubQuery

docs.title: Determinism Guarantees
docs.text:
• Stable IDs are generated via SHA‑256 hash of sub‑query content; identical sub‑queries are told apart by an ordinal suffix (_2, _3, ...).
  • Ordering of outputs is explicitly sorted.
  • LLM output is non‑deterministic unless configured deterministically.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Emits PipelineError with:

  • PLANNER_FAILED when a decomposition is rejected twice (step 8), with the reason;
  • PLANNER_FAILED when a join/compare combine group has fewer than two inputs (step 5), for example because RBAC dropped one side;
  • ORCHESTRATOR_CRASH on exceptions; a provider's refusal of the call is a PROVIDER_* error instead (see provider failures).

Logs failures via logger.error.

docs.title: Retry + Idempotency
docs.text:
• One internal retry: a decomposition whose post-combine op reads a column its combine group will not produce is asked for again, once, with the reason (step 8). When recording, the retry's answer replaces the first under the same question, so replay serves the corrected decomposition.
  • Idempotent for fixed LLM output; otherwise LLM variability can change output.

docs.title: Performance Characteristics
docs.text:
• One LLM call per pipeline execution.
  • Hashing and sorting are in‑memory and low cost.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
• Logger: decomposer
  • Adds a reasoning entry on completion or failure.

  • Replace or wrap node in build_graph() for custom behavior.

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
• No fallback when LLM fails.
  • Output quality depends on LLM configuration and prompt.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Executes the ExecutionDAG over persisted artifacts using the aggregation engine.
  • Exists to combine scan results deterministically into final result sets.
  • Sits after layer_router and before AnswerSynthesizerNode.
  • Class: EngineAggregatorNode
  • Source: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/aggregator/node.py

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Load scan artifacts from artifact_refs, lazily, as polars scans.
  • Execute combine and post‑operation nodes in DAG order, as one lazy plan.
  • Save each terminal result as its own artifact, and produce AggregatorResponse with those artifacts and a preview of each.

docs.title: Position in Execution Graph
docs.text:
Upstream: - layer_router (after all scan artifacts are available)

Downstream: - AnswerSynthesizerNode, when aggregation succeeded - End of run, when it failed (aggregator_route in pipeline/routes.py)

Trigger conditions: - Router dispatches to aggregator when no pending scan nodes remain.

flowchart LR
    Router[layer_router] --> Aggregator[EngineAggregatorNode] --> Synth[AnswerSynthesizerNode]

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
From GraphState:

  • execution_dag (required)
  • artifact_refs (required)

Validation performed:

  • None in node; aggregation service raises on missing artifacts.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Mutations to GraphState:

  • aggregator_response (AggregatorResponse)
  • reasoning and errors

Side effects:

  • Reads artifacts from the artifact store.
  • Writes one artifact per terminal result, in the run's folder: <tenant_id>/<request_id>/result_<node_id>.parquet with the default template (see Artifact Store).
  • Writes the run's result manifest beside them, <tenant_id>/<request_id>/manifest.json (see Artifact Store).

docs.title: Internal Flow (Step-by-Step)
docs.text:
1. Read execution_dag and artifact_refs.
  2. Check every combine input against its row cap (see Row cap before a combine below). A capped input to a join/compare ends the run here with RESULT_TRUNCATED; a capped input to a union adds a RESULT_TRUNCATED warning and aggregation goes on.
  3. Invoke AggregationService.execute(dag, artifact_refs).
  4. A join/compare combine resolves each join key against its frame's columns. A key written with a side or sub-query prefix (right.customer, sq_2.customer) resolves to the bare column when only that exists; an unknown key is left for polars to report. A join/compare with fewer than two inputs raises (AGGREGATOR_FAILED) instead of returning the one frame it has; the decomposer refuses such a group before anything runs, so this is the last line of defence.
  5. A post-combine op (PolarsDuckdbEngine.post_op) applies every field it carries, in SQL's order: the reshaping its operation names (aggregate groups with polars' group_by, project selects expected_schema), then its filters (after an aggregate they filter the aggregated rows, as HAVING does), its order_by, and its limit. A filter op with order_by and limit, as the decomposer's prompt used to show, keeps all three.
  6. Before polars is asked for any column, a post-combine op's attributes (group_by, metrics, project's expected_schema, filters, order_by) are checked against the combined frame. An attribute the frame does not have is refused with the columns it does have, and a side-qualified one (right.customer) with the reason — see No anti-join below. The decomposer runs the same check on the decomposition before anything executes (nl2sql/aggregation/columns.py, shared with this engine) and asks the model again once, so here it is the last line of defence.
  7. AggregationService.execute returns each terminal node as a polars LazyFrame: the scans are ArtifactStore.scan_parquet, and the combines and post-combine ops only add to the plan, so no sub-query result is loaded whole before it is written.
  8. Save each terminal result with ArtifactStore.write_lazy, which streams the plan into a parquet artifact, and build AggregatorResponse:
  9. computed_artifacts[node_id]: the saved result's ArtifactRef, with the whole result's row_count and columns (sub_query_id unset).
  10. results: one ResultSummary per saved result (node_id, columns, row_count, and truncated: a sub-query upstream of the node in the DAG was cut at its row cap), also written as the run's manifest.json. QueryResult.result_manifest carries it, and the facade's paging and CSV export read the result by it.
  11. terminal_results[node_id]: the first settings.results.preview_rows rows, read back from that artifact. This is what the answer model is shown; it is not the whole result.
  12. Return success reasoning.
  13. On exception, emit AGGREGATOR_FAILED, on the state's errors and on AggregatorResponse.errors. The graph's aggregator_route then ends the run: the answer synthesizer is not called on the empty result, so the aggregator's error is the run's outcome and no model call is spent explaining {}.

docs.title: Row cap before a combine
docs.text:
The generator caps every sub-query at its datasource's row_limit, bounded by the settings.results.row_limit ceiling (100,000, also the cap when none is set), unless the plan asks for fewer rows itself, and records that cap as row_cap on its response and on the sub-query's SubgraphOutput. The cap is applied in each sub-query's SQL, before the combine: a join input with 2240 rows under a row_limit of 1000 reaches the aggregator as 1000, and every match the other 1240 held is silently lost. The wrapper marks such a sub-query's SubgraphOutput.truncated, which QueryResult and the answer carry (see AnswerSynthesizerNode).

So before combining, the aggregator looks at each combine input whose result has row_cap rows or more:

  • join / compare: refused. The run ends with RESULT_TRUNCATED (through aggregator_route, so no answer is synthesized), naming the sub-query and the cap. Missing rows mean missing matches, so the combined answer could be wrong, and a wrong answer is worse than none.
  • union: a warning. The rows a union returns are still right, only possibly incomplete, so it runs and a RESULT_TRUNCATED warning with the sub-query's id is carried to QueryResult.warnings.

A result of exactly row_cap rows may be complete; telling the two apart would mean fetching one row more, so it is treated as cut short. A plan's own top-N (LIMIT 5) is the answer, not truncation, and is never flagged. To answer such a question, ask something narrower (aggregate in the sub-query) or raise the datasource's row_limit.

docs.title: No anti-join: what "bought X but never Y" does here
docs.text:
CombineGroup.operation is one of standalone, compare, join and union. join and compare are both inner joins (how="inner" in PolarsDuckdbEngine.combine), and FilterSpec has no null or existence operator, so there is no way to express "present on the left and absent on the right". This is a capability gap in the plan language, not a bug in the engine.

Asked "Which customers bought jazz tracks but never rock?", the model decomposes it into the two sets and then reaches for a right-hand column to negate against — right.customer. That column does not exist: an inner join keyed on the shared column drops the right-hand copy, and the other right-hand columns are suffixed _right. Every tier 2 run has failed this question, and what reached the caller was polars' own unable to find column "right.customer"; valid columns: ["customer"].

Resolving the prefix away would be worse. right.customer would become customer, the filter would run against the intersection, and the answer would be the customers who bought both genres — wrong, and silently so. So the attribute check refuses the question and says why. The decomposer now makes this check first and asks the model once more with the same message; a second answer with the same problem ends the run in the decomposer with it, before any scan runs. A recording run also met the made-up variant, a filter on bought_rock, which the same check catches. The message reads:

Aggregator failed: Post-combine operation references 'right.customer', which
the combined result does not have. Available columns: customer. A column
qualified by side does not survive the combine: ... it cannot be expressed:
the plan language has no anti-join or set-difference operation ... so the
question is refused rather than answered with the intersection.

The same gap has a second shape: the decomposer sometimes emits the two sub-queries uncombined, and AggregationService.execute then returns two terminal result sets, which the run reports as "expected one result set, got 2" (2026-09-22_27cad30). Both are the same missing operation.

Closing it properly means adding an anti-join (or except) to CombineGroup.operation, the decomposer prompt, the DAG and the engine. That is a feature, not a fix, and is deliberately not done here.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Delegates SQL execution to an executor service based on datasource capabilities.
  • Persists results via the artifact store and returns ExecutorResponse.
  • Sits after GeneratorNode in the SQL agent subgraph.
  • Class: ExecutorNode
  • Source: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/executor/node.py

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Validate required execution inputs (SQL and datasource ID).
  • Gate execution on the datasource declaring supports_sql.
  • Build and submit ExecutorRequest.
  • Return executor response and propagate errors.

docs.title: Position in Execution Graph
docs.text:
Upstream: - GeneratorNode

Downstream: - Subgraph end (artifacts returned to control graph).

Trigger conditions: - Executed when SQL generation succeeds.

flowchart LR
    Generator[GeneratorNode] --> Executor[ExecutorNode] --> EndNode[SubgraphEnd]

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
From SubgraphExecutionState:

  • generator_response.sql_draft (required)
  • sub_query.datasource_id (required)
  • sub_query.schema_version (optional)
  • trace_id, subgraph_name, user_context

From Runtime:

  • ds_registry
  • tenant_id

Validation performed:

  • Missing SQL → MISSING_SQL
  • Missing datasource ID → MISSING_DATASOURCE_ID
  • No executor for datasource → INVALID_STATE

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Mutations to SubgraphExecutionState:

  • executor_response (ExecutorResponse)
  • errors and reasoning

Side effects:

  • Executes SQL against datasource via executor service.
  • Reads the result a batch at a time when the adapter has execute_batches (StreamingAdapterProtocol), settings.results.fetch_batch_size rows per batch, and writes each batch to the artifact as it arrives (ArtifactStore.write_batches); an adapter without it is called through execute and its one frame is written the same way. A failure the adapter reports between batches fails the sub-query as a failed execute would, and nothing is written (see artifact store). metrics.row_count and metrics.bytes_returned are summed over the batches.
  • SqlExecutorService also takes ExecutorRequest.parameters and max_rows, which this node never sets: generated SQL carries no parameters and its LIMIT is in the text. The curated matcher sets both for a verified query: the parameters reach the adapter in AdapterRequest.parameters and are bound, and the stream stops after max_rows rows, cutting the last batch and closing the adapter's stream.
  • Persists results to artifact store, one artifact per sub-query: the request's node_id (the sub-query id) is passed to the store as sub_query_id and dag_node_id, so two sub-queries of one run never write the same file (see artifact store). The ArtifactRef records it as sub_query_id.

docs.title: Internal Flow (Step-by-Step)
docs.text:
1. Validate SQL and datasource ID.
  2. Check the adapter declares supports_sql; otherwise return INVALID_STATE.
  3. Build ExecutorRequest with trace/subgraph identifiers and schema version.
  4. Execute request and return ExecutorResponse.
  5. If the query succeeded with no rows, check the filter values (below).
  6. On exception, emit EXECUTOR_CRASH.

docs.title: An empty result's filter values
docs.text:
"Which customers bought Metal?" planned as Genre.Name = 'Metal' returns no rows because Chinook's genre is 'Heavy Metal'. Reported as is, the answer says nobody bought any. So when a query succeeds with zero rows, value_check.check_values() looks at every string literal the plan's WHERE compares a bare column to with =, IN or LIKE, through AND and OR only (a negated or != comparison, a column inside a function, and a number are left alone), at most five per sub-query:

  1. Does it exist? SELECT 1 FROM <table> WHERE <column> = '<value>' LIMIT 1 (LIKE for a pattern). If yes, nothing is said: the empty result stands.
  2. The closest values. A case-insensitive match first (LOWER(column) = LOWER('value'), DISTINCT, LIMIT 3); failing that, a bounded SELECT DISTINCT column ... LIMIT n (n is 500, or the adapter's row_limit if lower) and the three most similar by difflib (cutoff 0.6).
  3. What it reports, as VALUE_NOT_FOUND:
  4. With a close value and a retry left, an ERROR telling the planner which values exist: "No Genre.Name value is 'Jaz', so the query returned no rows. The closest existing values are 'Jazz'; use one of them if it is what the question means." The SQL agent sends it back through the refiner (see SQL agent). It is raised once per sub-query: an empty result after that retry is reported as a warning instead.
  5. Otherwise a WARNING: "There is no Genre with Name 'Polka'." (with "; the closest is ..." when there is one). The sub-query still succeeds with its empty result, and the answer synthesizer is told the value does not exist (see AnswerSynthesizerNode).

Every probe is a SELECT built with sqlglot and rendered by the adapter (render_sql), so no dialect is named here; each has a LIMIT no higher than the adapter's row cap. A table the role may not read (RBAC, as the logical validator checks it) is never probed, a probe the database refuses claims nothing, and a failure in the check never fails the run.

docs.title: Contracts & Interfaces
docs.text:
Implements a LangGraph node callable:

def __call__(self, state: SubgraphExecutionState) -> Dict[str, Any]

Key contracts:

  • ExecutorRequest
  • ExecutorResponse

docs.title: Determinism Guarantees
docs.text:
• Deterministic request construction.
  • Execution results depend on external datasource state and are not deterministic.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Emits PipelineError with:

  • MISSING_SQL
  • MISSING_DATASOURCE_ID
  • INVALID_STATE
  • EXECUTION_FAILED: the database rejected the query as wrong (the adapter's retryable); the SQL agent sends it back to the refiner while retries remain
  • DB_EXECUTION_ERROR: the database refused or could not run the query (permission, timeout, connection); fatal
  • EXECUTOR_CRASH: an exception escaped the adapter
  • VALUE_NOT_FOUND: an empty result filtered on a value its column does not have; an ERROR (retried once) when a close value exists, a WARNING otherwise

docs.title: Retry + Idempotency
docs.text:
• No internal retry logic. The SQL agent's check_execution routes a retryable EXECUTION_FAILED back to the refiner (see SQL agent).
  • Idempotency depends on datasource and query semantics.

docs.title: Performance Characteristics
docs.text:
• External I/O dominates (database execution).
  • Artifact persistence writes Parquet results.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
• Logger: executor
  • Propagates executor response reasoning and errors.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
• tenant_id from settings.
  • Executor selection based on adapter capabilities.

docs.title: Extension Points
docs.text:
• Extend SqlExecutorService to alter execution behavior.
  • Replace node in build_sql_agent_graph() to alter execution behavior.

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
• Executes in‑process on the pipeline thread pool; there is no process sandbox (see ../../execution/isolation.md).
  • No built‑in retries on transient execution failures.
  • The filter-value check covers string literals in WHERE only, not HAVING, and reads at most 500 distinct values to find a similar one, so on a high-cardinality column a near miss can go unsuggested (the value is then reported as missing).

  • Build a SQL query with ordered selects, joins, filters, groupings, and limits.
  • Apply adapter dialect and row limit.

From Runtime:

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:

  • generator_response (GeneratorResponse with sql_draft, and row_cap: the adapter's row_limit when it, not the plan's own LIMIT, bounds the query; None when the plan asked for that many rows or fewer). The aggregator uses it to tell a sub-query cut short by the cap from a complete one (see EngineAggregatorNode).
  • reasoning
  • errors on failure

  • Adapter registry access for dialect/limits.

docs.title: Internal Flow (Step-by-Step)
docs.text:
1. Validate presence of datasource ID and plan.
  2. Resolve adapter and dialect.
  3. Compute effective limit from plan/adapter row limit: row_limit is the datasource's row_limit bounded by the settings.results.row_limit ceiling (100,000), or the ceiling when the datasource sets none; the limit is min(plan.limit or row_limit, row_limit). When the cap is what bounds the query, record it as row_cap.
  4. Traverse AST with SqlVisitor to build sqlglot expression tree.
  5. Every operator becomes the node sqlglot's parser would build (+ -> exp.Add, * -> exp.Mul, IS NOT -> NOT ... IS ..., and so on), wherever it is nested. An operator with no mapping raises; it is never rendered as a function named after the operator.
  6. An operand that is itself an operator is parenthesised, because sqlglot prints a hand-built tree without adding the parentheses its parser would have seen ((a + b) * c would otherwise print as a + b * c).
  7. / is sqlglot's true division, so on SQLite it renders as CAST(a AS REAL) / b rather than integer division.
  8. || is string concatenation, rendered as the dialect's own: a || b on SQLite and Postgres, CONCAT(a, b) on MySQL, a + b on T-SQL. A + with a string operand (a non-numeric string literal, or another concatenation) renders the same way, because on SQLite 'Jane' + ' ' is numeric addition and returns 0. A + between two columns stays addition: their types are not known here.
  9. Select aliases and column names are quoted, the dialect's way, only when they are not bare identifiers. The decomposer names result columns in plain words and the planner must use those names as aliases, so an alias such as sales support agent renders as AS "sales support agent" (and AS `sales support agent` on MySQL), in the select list and in the ORDER BY tie-breakers.
  10. A func expr with distinct: true wraps its arguments in exp.Distinct, so {"kind": "func", "func_name": "COUNT", "is_aggregate": true, "distinct": true, "args": [x]} renders as COUNT(DISTINCT x). PlanModel.distinct: true renders SELECT DISTINCT.
  11. A func expr is built with sqlglot.exp.func(name, *args), so a function sqlglot knows becomes its typed node and each dialect renders it its own way (LENGTH is LEN on T-SQL, COUNT is COUNT_BIG on T-SQL). A name sqlglot does not know (such as STRFTIME) stays as written; the logical validator has already limited names to ast_planner.functions.ALLOWED_FUNCTIONS. A function sqlglot builds as an operator (MOD(a, b) is a % b) keeps its operands' grouping.
  12. Dates are portable: DATE_PART(unit, x) becomes CAST(EXTRACT(unit FROM x) AS INT), an integer, and DATE_TRUNC(unit, x) becomes exp.TimeToStr(exp.TimestampTrunc(x, unit), '%Y-%m-%d'), a YYYY-MM-DD string, with unit year, quarter, month or day. YEAR(x), QUARTER(x), MONTH(x), DAY(x), EXTRACT(unit, x) and DATE_TRUNC(x, unit) written by a model are read the same way. The generator writes no dialect SQL for them: the adapter renders the tree (next step).
  13. Attach joins. The first table in plan.tables is the FROM table. left_alias/right_alias do not say which table is new: each join attaches whichever side is not yet in scope, taking the first listed join that touches a table already in scope, so joins may be listed in any order. When the new table is the join's left side, left/right outer joins are mirrored so the same table is preserved. Joined tables keep their schema_name/database qualifiers.
  14. Order the rows completely. The plan's ORDER BY terms come first, with their direction. Every other selected column follows as an ascending tie-breaker, in select order. With no ORDER BY in the plan, the query is ordered by every selected column. This does not change what the query means, but without it the LIMIT below could keep a different subset of rows on each run.
  15. An aliased item is ordered by its alias (ORDER BY genre, track_sales), which stays valid for aggregates under GROUP BY. Terms are never positions.
  16. A select item already used as an ORDER BY term, by expression or by alias, is not repeated.
  17. Constant items are skipped: they order nothing, and a bare number would be read as a position.
  18. Every term, the plan's own and the tie-breakers, keeps the dialect's default NULL placement for its direction, so no NULLS FIRST/NULLS LAST clause is rendered (nor, on T-SQL and MySQL, a CASE WHEN ... IS NULL emulation, which is invalid when the term is an alias). For example, a plan ordering by city ascending and c.Country descending renders ORDER BY city ASC, c.Country DESC, c.LastName on SQLite, Postgres, T-SQL and MySQL alike.
  19. The logical validator runs on the plan before this step and never sees the tie-breakers.
  20. Apply the effective limit, then the plan's offset when it is above zero: rows 11 to 20 are limit: 10, offset: 10. The limit is already capped, so a page is never longer than the row cap, and row_cap is reported exactly as without an offset. sqlglot renders the pair in each dialect's own form (LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10; OFFSET 10 ROWS FETCH FIRST 10 ROWS ONLY on T-SQL). An offset only means something in an order, so a plan with an offset and no order_by, or a negative offset, is refused here with a ValueError; the logical validator runs this builder, so the planner is asked to fix it before generation (see Buildability). The tie-breakers of step 6 then make the page the same on every run.
  21. Hand the finished tree to the adapter's render_sql(expression) (see the SDK). An adapter without the hook is rendered with query.sql(dialect=adapter.get_dialect()). The SQLite adapter rewrites the date nodes with STRFTIME/DATE(x, 'start of ...'); the others use sqlglot's rendering.
  22. Return GeneratorResponse with SQL and reasoning.
  23. On exception, emit SQL_GEN_FAILED.

docs.text:
Implements a LangGraph node callable:

def __call__(self, state: SubgraphExecutionState) -> Dict[str, Any]

Key contracts:

  • GeneratorResponse
  • PlanModel / Expr

docs.title: Determinism Guarantees
docs.text:
• Deterministic for a fixed AST and adapter dialect.
  • Ordering is the plan's own list order: the first select item is the first column, the first table is the FROM table.
  • Row order is total: every selected column is an ORDER BY term (see step 6), so the same plan run against the same data returns the same rows in the same order, even when LIMIT truncates the result.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Emits PipelineError with:

  • SQL_GEN_FAILED

A malformed join graph is a planning error, not something to guess around. SQL_GEN_FAILED is raised when a join names an undeclared alias, when a join connects two tables that are both already in scope, when a join cannot be reached from the FROM table, or when a declared table is never joined.

In practice the planner should never see this. There is no retry edge after the generator, so a SQL_GEN_FAILED ends the sub-query. LogicalValidatorNode therefore runs _build_query() itself and reports the same ValueError as a retryable INVALID_PLAN_STRUCTURE one node earlier — see Buildability. The checks below stay where they are: they are the single definition of the rules, and the validator calling this code is what keeps the two in step. SUPPORTED_BINARY_OPS is exported for the same reason — it is the set SqlVisitor._visit_binary renders, and the validator rejects anything outside it before the plan gets here.

Logs exceptions via logger.exception.

docs.text:
• No internal retry logic.
  • Idempotent for a fixed plan.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Validates the AST plan (PlanModel) against schema and RBAC policies.
  • Exists to enforce correctness and security before SQL generation.
  • Sits between ASTPlannerNode and GeneratorNode in the SQL agent subgraph.
  • Class: LogicalValidatorNode
  • Source: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/validator/node.py

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Validate aliases, joins, and column references.
  • Reject any plan the generator could not build (see Buildability below).
  • Enforce RBAC table access using strict datasource namespacing.

Literal filter values are not validated against a column's sampled values. The adapter records every value of a text column with at most 50 distinct values, but only the five most frequent of a larger one: a retrieval hint, not the column's domain. Treating it as an allowlist rejected correct filters on any higher-cardinality column. Safety comes from the RBAC table allowlist and from schema resolution, neither of which depends on stats. A value that turns out not to exist is caught after execution instead, and only when the result is empty (see ExecutorNode).

docs.title: Buildability: the validator runs the generator
docs.text:
_validate_columns() resolves columns against a query in which every plan table is CROSS JOINed (_build_validation_query()). That is correct for column resolution — alias-to-column visibility does not depend on join structure — and it is exactly why the validator is blind to join topology.

The generator builds the real FROM clause and walks the join graph, so four structural mistakes used to pass validation CLEAN and fail one node later as a terminal SQL_GEN_FAILED: a declared table never joined to the FROM table, a plan with several tables and no joins at all, a join island that does not connect to the FROM table, and the same pair joined twice. GeneratorNode has no retry edge after it, so each of those ended the sub-query with no chance for the planner to fix it.

Rather than restate those four rules here and let the two drift apart, _validate_buildable() calls GeneratorNode._build_query() with the sub-query's own datasource dialect and discards the tree. Any ValueError becomes a retryable INVALID_PLAN_STRUCTURE, and the message is extended with the plan's tables and the foreign keys declared between them, written with the plan's own aliases — the same move _describe_column_failure() makes for columns:

Table alias(es) t3 are declared in the plan but never joined to the FROM table.
Plan tables: t1 = Artist, t2 = Album, t3 = Track.
Foreign keys between them: t2 (Album).ArtistId = t1 (Artist).ArtistId;
t3 (Track).AlbumId = t2 (Album).AlbumId.

It runs last, after every other static check, so each of those keeps its own error code and the generator's wording never replaces a more specific one. The cost is a second tree build, measured at ~2.4 ms against a ~3.4 s planner call.

test_logical_validator_generator_parity.py asserts the invariant directly: for each broken plan shape, the generator rejects it and so does the validator. The same route rejects an offset with no order_by, or a negative one (test_plan_offset.py): a page only means something in an order.

Column resolution is delegated to sqlglot's optimizer. The node converts the plan into a throw‑away sqlglot expression tree (reusing the generator's SqlVisitor) and runs sqlglot.optimizer.qualify.qualify() against a schema built from relevant_tables. The LLM contract is unchanged: the planner still emits a PlanModel, never SQL.

docs.text:
Upstream: - ASTPlannerNode

Downstream: - GeneratorNode on success - retry_handler on retryable errors

Trigger conditions: - Executed when an AST plan is present.

flowchart LR
    Planner[ASTPlannerNode] --> Validator[LogicalValidatorNode] --> Generator[GeneratorNode]
    Validator --> RetryHandler[retry_handler]

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
From SubgraphExecutionState:

  • ast_planner_response.plan (required)
  • relevant_tables (required)
  • user_context (required for RBAC)
  • sub_query.datasource_id (required for namespacing)
  • sub_query.expected_schema (optional validation)

Validation performed:

  • Aliases must be unique.
  • Joins must match known relationships.
  • Column references must exist and be unambiguous.
  • Every binary operator must be one the generator can render.
  • The plan must build into a query at all.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Mutations to SubgraphExecutionState:

  • logical_validator_response (LogicalValidatorResponse, carrying errors, reasoning and checks)
  • errors and reasoning

checks is a List[ValidationCheck] (name, passed, message) recording what was validated, not only what failed. The names are fixed and always in this order:

name meaning plan_present A plan reached the validator. The only check emitted when it did not. structure_and_schema Tables, columns and joins resolve against the retrieved schema. policy Every table in the plan is allowed for the caller's role.

On failure the check's message is the first corresponding error's message.

Side effects:

  • None beyond in‑memory validation.

docs.title: Internal Flow (Step-by-Step)
docs.text:
1. If plan is missing, emit MISSING_PLAN and stop.
  2. Run _validate_static() for structural checks:
  3. _resolve_plan_tables() maps each plan alias to its schema columns and emits TABLE_NOT_FOUND for unknown tables. This stays hand-written because qualify() silently ignores relations absent from its schema.
  4. _distinct_function() rejects a func expr named DISTINCT with INVALID_PLAN_STRUCTURE: COUNT(DISTINCT x) is distinct: true on the COUNT expr, and SELECT DISTINCT is PlanModel.distinct.
  5. _unsupported_functions() rejects every other func name that is not a plain identifier (^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$) naming a function in ast_planner.functions.ALLOWED_FUNCTIONS (read-only aggregates and scalar functions, any case), with UNSUPPORTED_FUNCTION at ERROR severity, so the refiner retries with the list in the message. The list leaves out LEGACY_FUNCTIONS (STRFTIME), which older plans may still call but which the planner prompt never offers. func_name becomes the function's name in the SQL, so this is what keeps model text such as SELECT 1); DELETE FROM T; -- out of it.
  6. _date_operations() rejects a date function whose unit is not year, quarter, month or day, or whose shape is not (unit literal, date), with INVALID_PLAN_STRUCTURE; the message states the portable forms.
  7. _unsupported_operators() rejects a binary op the generator's SqlVisitor cannot render, with INVALID_PLAN_STRUCTURE. The schema's op Literal admits NOT, which belongs on a unary expression; every other member is in generator.node.SUPPORTED_BINARY_OPS. This runs before any check that walks the plan through the visitor, because an operator it cannot render makes all of them raise — which is how op: "NOT" used to surface as a VALIDATOR_CRASH.
  8. _validate_columns() builds the plan's sqlglot tree and runs qualify(..., validate_qualify_columns=True). On failure each distinct column reference is re-probed so every bad reference is reported, and _describe_column_failure() rewrites the optimizer's SQL-oriented text into plan-oriented feedback the refiner can act on. ORDER BY terms are wrapped in exp.Ordered first (generator.node.ordered()): sqlglot only wraps an argument it has to parse, and a bare function node in Order.expressions makes qualify() raise.
  9. _validate_buildable() runs last and is the buildability check: it calls the generator's own _build_query() and throws the tree away. See below.
  10. Run _validate_policy() for RBAC enforcement. This always runs, even when static validation failed or raised — the security check is never skipped. Each forbidden table yields a CRITICAL SECURITY_VIOLATION whose message is "You do not have permission to see the data this question requires." (it names nothing), with details = {datasource_id, table, roles} for the trace, and a warning log line. policies.refusal_names_tables: true puts the role and table in the message instead. An unknown role, or no role, allows no table and is refused the same way. The decision reads only the policy and the plan's table list, never the model's reasoning.
  11. If any errors are ERROR/CRITICAL, return with errors.
  12. Otherwise return success reasoning.
  13. On exception, emit VALIDATOR_CRASH.

docs.title: Internal Flow (Step-by-Step)
docs.text:
1. If no LLM configured, emit MISSING_LLM and stop.
  2. Render relevant tables with render_schema_for_prompt (the planner's compact schema block, only sample_values and the date and numeric columns' range from the column stats), and the failed plan as compact JSON (model_dump_json(exclude_none=True)).
  3. Build error and reasoning strings. The errors are the failed attempt's only, one line each as - [node] ERROR_CODE: message; earlier attempts' errors are not repeated.
  4. Invoke LLM with refinement prompt. It is two messages: the system message holds the instructions and then the schema (stable, so the provider can cache it); the human message holds the question, today's date (run_date(settings.pipeline.today), as the planner gets it), failed plan, errors and reasoning. On Chinook the prompt is about 2,600 tokens (was about 8,000), 2,500 of them a prefix shared across questions.
  5. Emit PLAN_FEEDBACK warning and return RefinerResponse.
  6. On exception, emit REFINER_FAILED.
