Without all three credentials the provider signs in with DefaultAzureCredential. nl2sql-engine[azure] hashicorp url and token (both required), mount_point (default secret) nl2sql-engine[hashicorp] env none none 
providers:
  - id: vault
    type: hashicorp
    url: "https://vault.internal:8200"
    token: "${env:VAULT_TOKEN}"

The settings are strict. An unknown or misspelt key, or a missing required one, fails when the config loads, and the message names the key.

A provider reads its settings from its entry only. It never falls back to an environment variable such as VAULT_ADDR, VAULT_TOKEN or AZURE_KEYVAULT_URL: when a value comes from the environment, write the field as an ${env:...} reference, as token does above.

The HashiCorp key is the secret's path and, after a colon, the field: ${vault:apps/sales:password} reads the field password of apps/sales in the KV version 2 engine at mount_point. Without a colon it reads the field value.

Each provider implements the SecretProvider interface from the SDK; see SDK reference → SecretProvider.

docs.title: Secret references
docs.text: Use ${provider_id:key} to resolve a secret from a provider, and ${env:VAR} to read an environment variable. A reference is the whole value. Every api_key and every value under a datasource's connection keep the reference until the component is built, so engine.config, logs and errors never hold the secret. Inside secrets: itself only ${env:...} is allowed: one provider cannot depend on another. See Configuration System → references.

docs.title: When a provider fails to start
docs.text:
A provider in the secrets section that cannot start fails startup at once: building the engine raises a ConfigError naming secrets.providers[i] (the CLI, nl2sql-api and nl2sql doctor print it). The error names the provider and the reason:

Secret provider 'vault' (type 'hashicorp') failed to start: Missing dependency 'hvac'.
Install 'nl2sql-engine[hashicorp]'. Fix or remove this entry in the secrets config.

The usual reasons are the provider's extra not being installed (nl2sql-engine[aws], [azure], [hashicorp]), a ${env:VAR} credential whose variable is not set (the message names the variable), or the provider's own client refusing the config. Credentials are masked in the message.

This is deliberate: every ${vault:...} reference depends on the provider, so starting without it only moves the error to the first lookup, where it reads as "Unknown secret provider ID". A config without a secrets section and the built-in env provider are unaffected. A datasource that fails to start, by contrast, leaves the others running: see Datasources → When a datasource fails to start.

docs.title: Secrets never print
docs.text:
A credential written as a value never prints: repr, str, log lines and tracebacks of the config show ********** instead. A ${provider:key} reference is not a secret and is shown as written. This covers:

  • api_key in llm, in each of llm.agents, and in embeddings, including a key the demo gives the engine in memory (nl2sql demo --api-key, or one saved in the playground's settings panel): repr(engine.config) never shows it;
  • in the secrets section, every provider setting whose name contains password, secret, token or api_key (client_secret for Azure, token for HashiCorp); the URL and the other settings still show;
  • in a datasource's connection, every field whose name contains one of the same words;
  • the resolved key the LLM registry builds a client from (AgentConfig, a pydantic SecretStr), including model_dump(mode="json") and model_dump_json().

The config's own fields stay plain strings, so the engine (and config.model_dump()) reads the real value; only printing masks it. A config built in code that fails validation never echoes its input either: the error names the field and the problem, not the value.

The real value is read only where it is used: building the LLM or embeddings client, a database connection, the artifact store's storage options or a secret provider's client. nl2sql init never writes a key: a key belongs in the environment or the .env next to nl2sql.yaml. The demo and the playground's Settings page save a key to that .env only, with its real value.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
The settings section of nl2sql.yaml holds the tuning knobs. It is optional, and every field has a default, so most configs leave it out. Each value is the engine's own: two engines in one process can run with different settings.

# settings.yaml (every value shown is the default)
tenant_id: default_tenant
pipeline:
  timeout_s: 60
  plan_cache: true
  strict_columns: true
  today: null                 # pin the run date: 2013-12-31
  retries: { max: 3, base_delay_s: 1.0, max_delay_s: 10.0, jitter_s: 0.5 }
retrieval:
  full_snapshot_max_tables: 15
results:
  row_limit: 100000
  fetch_batch_size: 10000
  preview_rows: 20
traces:
  mode: on_failure            # off | on_failure | always
  sample_rows: 50
  max_field_chars: 20000
schema:
  max_versions: 3
  version_mismatch: warn      # warn | fail | ignore
curated:
  match_top_k: 5
  match_floor: 0.6
feedback:
  enabled: true
observability:
  exporter: none              # none | console | otlp
  otlp_endpoint: null

Unknown keys are errors, as everywhere in the config. The demo (nl2sql init --demo) writes a settings.yaml with pipeline.timeout_s: 300 (a live run makes six model calls; one OpenAI run took 136 s) and traces.mode: always (the playground's Debug drill-down reads every run's trace).

In Python, the groups are Settings, PipelineSettings, RetrySettings, RetrievalSettings, ResultSettings, TraceSettings, SchemaSettings, CuratedSettings, FeedbackSettings and ObservabilitySettings in nl2sql.config. The schema group is the attribute schema_ (cfg.settings.schema_.max_versions), because schema would shadow a pydantic method; the YAML key is schema.

docs.title: tenant_id
docs.text: The tenant id for requests that name none. Result files are kept per tenant.

docs.title: pipeline
docs.text: Key Default Description timeout_s 60 Timeout in seconds for one question. The caller is answered within about a second of the limit; the run's worker thread winds down in the background (see isolation). plan_cache true Reuse a plan that already passed validation and executed, for the same normalised sub-query intent, datasource and schema version on the same run date, instead of calling the planner LLM. The cached plan is validated again on every use, so RBAC and policy changes still apply. Stored in <storage.path>/state.db; nl2sql cache clear empties it. See Determinism → The plan cache. strict_columns true Treat a column the plan names but the retrieved schema does not have as a blocking, retryable COLUMN_NOT_FOUND error, so the planner is asked again instead of the plan reaching the database. false downgrades it to a warning that lets the plan through once retries are spent. today none The date the planner and refiner are told it is, as an ISO date (2013-12-31). Unset, it is the real date in UTC. Pin it for tests and gold runs whose questions say "this year" or "the last 30 days". A trace records the date its run used, and nl2sql trace replay pins it. It is part of the plan cache key, so a plan made on another date is not reused. retries.max 3 Retry attempts for the SQL agent's refinement loop. retries.base_delay_s 1.0 Base delay between retries, in seconds. retries.max_delay_s 10.0 Longest delay between retries. retries.jitter_s 0.5 Most jitter added to a delay.

docs.title: retrieval
docs.text: Key Default Description full_snapshot_max_tables 15 When a datasource's schema has at most this many tables, the schema retriever skips vector retrieval and passes the full schema snapshot (every table, every column) to the planner. 0 always uses vector retrieval.

docs.title: results
docs.text: Key Default Description row_limit 100000 The most rows one sub-query returns: a resource ceiling baked into the SQL as a LIMIT. A datasource's own limits.row_limit applies when it is lower (the demo datasources set 10000). A result that reaches it is flagged as truncated (QueryResult.truncated, sub_queries[].truncated) and the answer says it was cut. fetch_batch_size 10000 Rows fetched from the database and written to the sub-query's result file at a time, for an adapter that streams (every built-in SQL adapter does). At most one batch is held in memory. See Artifact Store. preview_rows 20 Result rows the answer model sees, with the total row count and the column names. The model writes about the result; it never copies it. See AnswerSynthesizerNode.

docs.title: traces
docs.text: Key Default Description mode on_failure When to write a run trace to <storage.path>/traces/: off, on_failure (errors, a retry, or an incomplete run) or always. See Debugging a Run. sample_rows 50 Result rows kept in a trace. max_field_chars 20000 Longest string kept in a node's recorded inputs and outputs; LLM prompts and responses are never cut.

docs.title: schema
docs.text: Key Default Description max_versions 3 Schema snapshots kept per datasource in <storage.path>/state.db. version_mismatch warn What to do when a plan's schema version is not the latest: warn, fail or ignore.

docs.title: curated
docs.text:
Key Default Description match_top_k 5 Verified query candidates a question's search returns, one per query. match_floor 0.6 Cosine similarity the best verified query candidate must reach before the model is asked to choose one. Below it the question is answered by the normal pipeline with no model call. See Curated Answers.

Whether curated answers are on is not a setting: the curated section is present or absent.

docs.title: feedback
docs.text: Key Default Description enabled true Let the playground record a thumbs up or down, with an optional note, for a run. Stored in <storage.path>/state.db: question, role, status, SQL, the datasources it ran on, whether the answer was verified or generated, error codes, the model per node and the engine version, never result rows or sample values. nl2sql feedback clear empties it. See Feedback and Signals.

docs.title: observability
docs.text: Key Default Description exporter none none, console or otlp. With otlp, the CLI and nl2sql-api also switch to JSON logs. otlp_endpoint none The OTLP endpoint.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
The storage section of nl2sql.yaml says where the engine keeps its data. It has one key:

# storage.yaml
path: .nl2sql          # or "${env:NL2SQL_DATA_DIR}" in a container

A relative path is relative to nl2sql.yaml in a file, and to the working directory when the Config is built in code. nl2sql init writes .nl2sql and adds .nl2sql/ to .gitignore.

Everything the engine writes lives under it:

Under path What Was (0.4) index/ The vector index (Chroma). The collection name is an internal constant. VECTOR_STORE, VECTOR_STORE_COLLECTION state.db SQLite: schema snapshots, the plan cache and playground feedback. SCHEMA_STORE_PATH traces/ Run traces (settings.traces.mode). TRACE_DIR results/ Result files, <tenant_id>/<request_id>/<sub_query_id>.parquet. See Artifact Store. RESULT_ARTIFACT_BASE_URI

Two engines with different paths share nothing. The commands that only read these stores (nl2sql cache clear, nl2sql feedback, nl2sql trace show) find them from the same config, so run them with the same --config.

Results are local files. The S3 and ADLS result backends of 0.4 were removed; remote stores come back with the results-store interface in a later release.

In a container, mount a volume and point the path at it:

path: "${env:NL2SQL_DATA_DIR}"

docker run -e NL2SQL_DATA_DIR=/data -v nl2sql-data:/data ...

docs.title: Configuration System
docs.text:
nl2sql reads one config: nl2sql.yaml and the files it includes. Loading it gives one typed Config object, and building that same Config in Python gives exactly the same engine. Everything the engine needs is in it. Only the config path and the provider key variables are read directly (see Environment variables); any other value from the environment is written in the YAML as ${env:VAR}.

The design and its reasoning are in Configuration v2. This page is the reference.

docs.title: nl2sql.yaml
docs.text:
nl2sql init writes a new project, with each section in its own file:

nl2sql init my-project              # an example SQLite datasource, allow_all policies
nl2sql init my-project --demo       # the demo: three sample databases, roles, verified queries
nl2sql init my-project --provider anthropic

nl2sql.yaml            # the table of contents
datasources/
  example.yaml         # one file per datasource (--demo: chinook.yaml, support.yaml, webanalytics.yaml)
llm.yaml               # provider + model; no key, the provider's standard variable is read
embeddings.yaml        # provider: local
policies.yaml          # allow_all: true            (--demo: admin, analyst, viewer roles)
storage.yaml           # path: .nl2sql
curated.yaml           # --demo only: the demo's verified queries
settings.yaml          # --demo only: the demo's tuning knobs
data/                  # --demo only: the three SQLite files, copied
.gitignore             # .nl2sql/ and .env

init refuses to overwrite a file without --force, never writes a key, and checks what it wrote with load_config.

# nl2sql.yaml
version: 2
datasources: { file: datasources/ }      # a folder, one file per datasource
llm:         { file: llm.yaml }
embeddings:  { file: embeddings.yaml }
policies:    { file: policies.yaml }
storage:     { file: storage.yaml }
curated:     { file: curated.yaml }      # optional
secrets:     { file: secrets.yaml }      # optional
settings:    { file: settings.yaml }     # optional
api:         { file: api.yaml }          # optional, read by nl2sql-api only

A small project can write every section inline instead. This file builds the same Config as a split layout would:

version: 2
datasources:
  - id: shop
    type: sqlite
    connection: { database: shop.db }
llm:        { provider: anthropic, model: claude-sonnet-5-5 }
embeddings: { provider: local }
policies:   { allow_all: true }
storage:    { path: .nl2sql }
Section Required Page Notes version yes 2. Anything else, or none, is an error that points to the 0.4 mapping. datasources yes Datasources A list; [] is enough. llm yes LLMs The model every agent uses, and per-agent overrides. embeddings yes Embeddings {provider: local} is a complete section. policies yes Policies {allow_all: true} is a complete section. storage yes Storage {path: .nl2sql} is a complete section. curated no Curated Answers Present means curated answers are on. secrets no Secrets The env provider is always there without it. settings no Settings Tuning knobs; every field has a default. api no REST API nl2sql-api's own settings; the engine ignores them.

From Python:

from nl2sql import NL2SQL, load_config

engine = NL2SQL.from_config("nl2sql.yaml")        # path=None: NL2SQL_CONFIG, then ./nl2sql.yaml
cfg = load_config("nl2sql.yaml")                  # the Config, to change in code first
engine = NL2SQL(cfg.model_copy(update={"settings": cfg.settings.model_copy(update={"tenant_id": "acme"})}))

See Public Facade → Creating an engine.

docs.title: file: includes
docs.text:
Rule Detail Shape A section is either inline, or exactly {file: <path>} with no other keys. Relative paths The path is relative to nl2sql.yaml, not to the working directory. One level Only nl2sql.yaml includes. An included file holds the section's body and includes nothing itself. No version Only nl2sql.yaml has version:. Datasource folder datasources: {file: datasources/} names a folder. Every *.yaml in it, sorted by name and not recursive, holds one datasource. id may be left out and defaults to the file name; if it is given, it must equal the file name. Datasource file datasources: {file: datasources.yaml} names a file whose body is the list. Literal paths file: values are never interpolated. Each file once Including the same file twice is an error.

Other relative paths are relative to nl2sql.yaml too: storage.path, and a SQLite or DuckDB database. The engine can be run from any working directory.

docs.title: Secret and variable references
docs.text:
${env:SALES_DB_PASSWORD} reads an environment variable; ${vault:apps/sales:password} reads a secret from the provider whose id is vault (see Secrets). env is built in.

Rule Detail Whole value only A reference is the entire string. "postgres://${env:U}@db" is an error, and there is no default syntax. Secrets resolve late Every api_key, the secret providers' credentials and every value under a datasource's connection keep the reference. It is resolved when the component is built, so engine.config, logs and errors never hold a plaintext secret. Everything else resolves at load Any other field, for example storage.path: "${env:NL2SQL_DATA_DIR}", is resolved by load_config. A variable that is not set is an error naming the field. Inside secrets: Only ${env:...}: one provider cannot depend on another.

docs.title: Strict keys and errors
docs.text:
Every section forbids unknown keys and suggests the closest known one. Names resolved through the registry (type:, provider:) suggest from the installed names. load_config and NL2SQL(...) collect every problem before raising one ConfigError, each naming the file it is in (an included file, not nl2sql.yaml):

nl2sql.yaml has 2 problems:

  datasources/sales.yaml → preferd_tables
    Unknown key. Did you mean 'preferred_tables'?

  llm.yaml → provider
    'antropic' is not an installed LLM provider. Did you mean 'anthropic'?

A secret is shown as its reference, never as its value. A 0.4 file (version: 1) gets one message pointing to the mapping.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
Only these are read directly:

Variable Read by Purpose NL2SQL_CONFIG load_config() with no path, the CLI, nl2sql-api Path to nl2sql.yaml. Without it, ./nl2sql.yaml. NL2SQL_LOG_LEVEL configure_logging() The log level when the caller passes none (DEBUG, INFO, ...). Without it, INFO. OPENAI_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, OPENROUTER_API_KEY nl2sql/llm/ The fallback key when llm.api_key (or an agent's, or embeddings.api_key) is not set.

Anything else from the environment is written in the YAML as ${env:VAR}. There are no generic overrides such as NL2SQL__SECTION__KEY. Third-party libraries (the OpenTelemetry SDK) still read their own standard variables, the trace redactor scans the environment for values to mask, and nl2sql benchmark checks CI. Nothing in nl2sql writes the environment: a key the demo is given travels in the engine's LLM config, and only the .env loading below adds variables. The architecture tests enforce both (invariants).

docs.title: .env files
docs.text:
Only the entry points load a .env file: the CLI, nl2sql-api and nl2sql demo load the .env next to nl2sql.yaml into the process environment at startup. A variable that is already set always wins; the file never overrides it. Each loads the .env before it configures logging, so a NL2SQL_LOG_LEVEL written there applies (nl2sql demo reads the demo project's .env, except with --hosted, which reads none).

The library itself never reads a .env file. A Python caller that wants one loads it before building the engine:

from dotenv import load_dotenv
from nl2sql import NL2SQL

load_dotenv("my-project/.env")   # or nl2sql.load_env_file("my-project/nl2sql.yaml")
engine = NL2SQL.from_config("my-project/nl2sql.yaml")

nl2sql init adds .env to .gitignore. Keep keys there, or in the environment, never in the YAML.

docs.title: The CLI
docs.text:
Every command reads the same config, named once, before the subcommand:

nl2sql --config prod/nl2sql.yaml index
nl2sql --config prod/nl2sql.yaml run "Top 5 customers by revenue"
NL2SQL_CONFIG=prod/nl2sql.yaml nl2sql curated validate
nl2sql run "..."                       # ./nl2sql.yaml

There are no per-command path flags. Commands that query or index build the engine and call engine.check() first (see Startup). nl2sql cache, nl2sql feedback and nl2sql trace show only need the store paths under storage.path, and build no engine.

docs.title: Checking a config: nl2sql config check
docs.text:
nl2sql config check checks the whole config without starting the engine, so it fits a CI job or a pre-deploy step:

nl2sql --config prod/nl2sql.yaml config check            # files, names, drivers
nl2sql --config prod/nl2sql.yaml config check --connect  # and connect to every datasource

It does what building the engine does, short of the stores:

  • reads nl2sql.yaml and every file it includes, and resolves ${env:...};
  • loads every name the config uses through the registry (type:, provider:, the secret providers): the name is installed, implements the interface version this engine needs, and its drivers are installed;
  • builds the components, which resolves each datasource's connection references, without connecting or calling a model.

With --connect it also connects to every datasource, as engine.check() does, and a datasource that fails is a problem (required or not).

Problems are printed by the file they are in, then a line per secret:

datasources/sales.yaml
  type
    Unknown adapter 'postgress'. Did you mean 'postgres'? Registered: duckdb, mssql, mysql, postgres, sqlite.

llm.yaml
  provider
    Unknown LLM provider 'antropic'. Did you mean 'anthropic'? Registered: anthropic, ollama, openai, openrouter.

Secrets:
  ${env:SALES_DB_PASSWORD} missing (datasources/sales.yaml → connection.password)

prod/nl2sql.yaml: 2 problems in 2 files.

A secret is reported as present or missing, never printed. Where the llm section names no api_key, the provider's standard variable is listed. A missing LLM key is reported but is not a problem, as for the engine: a CI job rarely holds the production key, and engine.check() reports it at startup. Any other secret that does not resolve stops the engine from building, so it is a problem.

Exit code Meaning 0 No problems. 1 One or more problems, or the config was not found. 2 A usage error: an unknown option.

The check creates no file under storage.path. From Python, the same check is nl2sql.config.check.check_config(path, registry=..., connect=...), which returns the problems, the secrets and the datasource statuses.

docs.title: Startup: check() and required
docs.text:
Building the engine never connects to a datasource or calls a model: every problem it can find without a connection is one ConfigError. engine.check() then connects to each datasource, checks that every agent's API key resolves (no model call) and reports the index status.

The CLI, nl2sql-api (in its lifespan, before it accepts requests) and nl2sql demo call check() at startup:

  • A datasource with required: true that fails, or datasources configured and none ready, raises EngineNotReady: the entry point prints the report and refuses to start (the CLI exits 1).
  • An optional datasource that fails is printed, left out of routing, and the entry point runs degraded.
# datasources/sales.yaml
type: postgres
required: true           # without it, nothing works: refuse to start
connection: { host: db.internal, database: sales, user: nl2sql, password: "${env:SALES_DB_PASSWORD}" }

A Python caller decides for itself. Without check(), a broken datasource fails the first query that targets it, with its reason.

docs.title: From 0.4
docs.text: 0.5 reads only nl2sql.yaml. There is no migration command: map each 0.4 file, variable and flag with these tables. nl2sql init writes a fresh layout to start from.

docs.title: Files
docs.text: 0.4 0.5 configs/datasources.yaml (DATASOURCE_CONFIG) datasources:, one file per datasource in datasources/. connection.type moves up to type; options: and the top-level limits become limits: {row_limit, timeout_ms, max_bytes}. configs/llm.yaml (LLM_CONFIG) llm:, flat: default:'s keys are the top level; agents: are keyed by node name (ast_planner, not astplanner); name: and version: are gone. configs/policies.json (POLICIES_CONFIG) policies:, in YAML; the role: field that repeated the key is gone. configs/secrets.yaml (SECRETS_CONFIG) secrets:, without version. hashi is now hashicorp. configs/curated.yaml (CURATED_CONFIG) curated:, without version. Present means on. configs/sample_questions.yaml (SAMPLE_QUESTIONS, ROUTING_EXAMPLES) sample_questions: on each datasource. .env, .env.<name> (ENV, APP_ENV, ENV_FILE_PATH) The .env next to nl2sql.yaml, loaded by the entry points only. .env.demo and configs/*.demo.* nl2sql init --demo (and nl2sql demo, which runs it): nl2sql.yaml, its files, and .env.

docs.title: Settings variables
docs.text: 0.4 variable 0.5 OPENAI_API_KEY llm.api_key / embeddings.api_key, or the fallback variable above VECTOR_STORE storage.path (the index is <path>/index/) VECTOR_STORE_COLLECTION removed (an internal constant) EMBEDDING_PROVIDER embeddings.provider EMBEDDING_MODEL embeddings.model TENANT_ID settings.tenant_id CURATED_ENABLED removed: the curated section is present or absent CURATED_MATCH_TOP_K settings.curated.match_top_k CURATED_MATCH_FLOOR settings.curated.match_floor GLOBAL_TIMEOUT_SEC settings.pipeline.timeout_s RESULT_ARTIFACT_BASE_URI storage.path (<path>/results/) RESULT_ARTIFACT_PATH_TEMPLATE removed: a fixed layout under <path>/results/ RESULT_ARTIFACT_BACKEND, RESULT_ARTIFACT_S3_*, RESULT_ARTIFACT_ADLS_* removed: results are local; the S3 and ADLS backends are deleted SCHEMA_STORE_BACKEND removed: SQLite at <path>/state.db SCHEMA_STORE_PATH storage.path (<path>/state.db, which also holds the plan cache and feedback) SCHEMA_STORE_MAX_VERSIONS settings.schema.max_versions SCHEMA_VERSION_MISMATCH_POLICY settings.schema.version_mismatch PLAN_CACHE_ENABLED settings.pipeline.plan_cache FEEDBACK_ENABLED settings.feedback.enabled SCHEMA_RETRIEVAL_FULL_SNAPSHOT_MAX_TABLES settings.retrieval.full_snapshot_max_tables LOGICAL_VALIDATOR_STRICT_COLUMNS settings.pipeline.strict_columns RBAC_REFUSAL_NAMES_TABLES policies.refusal_names_tables SQL_AGENT_MAX_RETRIES settings.pipeline.retries.max SQL_AGENT_RETRY_BASE_DELAY_SEC settings.pipeline.retries.base_delay_s SQL_AGENT_RETRY_MAX_DELAY_SEC settings.pipeline.retries.max_delay_s SQL_AGENT_RETRY_JITTER_SEC settings.pipeline.retries.jitter_s LLM_PRICES llm.prices TRACE_MODE settings.traces.mode TRACE_DIR storage.path (<path>/traces/) RESULT_ROW_LIMIT settings.results.row_limit RESULT_FETCH_BATCH_SIZE settings.results.fetch_batch_size ANSWER_PREVIEW_ROWS settings.results.preview_rows TRACE_SAMPLE_ROWS settings.traces.sample_rows TRACE_MAX_FIELD_CHARS settings.traces.max_field_chars NL2SQL_TODAY settings.pipeline.today OBSERVABILITY_EXPORTER settings.observability.exporter OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT settings.observability.otlp_endpoint

docs.title: Other variables
docs.text: 0.4 variable 0.5 NL2SQL_API_ROLE_HEADER api.role_header NL2SQL_API_ROLE api.role NL2SQL_API_TRUST_BODY_ROLE api.trust_body_role NL2SQL_API_CORS_ORIGINS (comma-separated) api.cors_origins (a list) NL2SQL_API_ADMIN_ROLES policies.admin_roles NL2SQL_DEMO_HOSTED nl2sql demo --hosted NL2SQL_DEMO_QUESTIONS_PER_MINUTE, NL2SQL_DEMO_QUESTIONS_PER_SESSION nl2sql demo --questions-per-minute N --questions-per-session N VAULT_ADDR, VAULT_TOKEN secrets.providers[].url / .token (write ${env:VAULT_TOKEN} to keep reading the variable) AZURE_KEYVAULT_URL secrets.providers[].vault_url ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, OPENROUTER_API_KEY unchanged: the fallback key variables CI unchanged: nl2sql benchmark refuses tier 2 in CI

docs.title: CLI
docs.text: 0.4 0.5 nl2sql setup nl2sql init [DIR] [--provider NAME] [--force]; the guided flow comes in a later release nl2sql setup --demo nl2sql init --demo [DIR] (or just nl2sql demo) --env NAME, --env-file PATH removed: the .env next to nl2sql.yaml is loaded --config PATH (the datasource file), --llm-config, --secrets-config, --policies-config, --vector-store the one global nl2sql --config PATH/nl2sql.yaml curated validate/test --curated --config --secrets nl2sql --config ... curated validate/test policy validate --config --policies --secrets nl2sql --config ... policy validate nl2sql --env demo <command> (from the demo folder) nl2sql --config nl2sql-demo/nl2sql.yaml <command>, or run it from inside nl2sql-demo/

docs.title: Source references
docs.text:
• Models and load_config: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/config/
  • init_project, demo_config: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/config/project.py
  • The runtime built from a Config: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/runtime.py
  • The CLI's --config: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/cli/common/engine.py
  • nl2sql config check: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/config/check.py, printed by packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/cli/commands/config_check.py

docs.title: Deployment Architecture
docs.text: NL2SQL is a Python engine that you embed in a service of your choice, or run as nl2sql-api. The runtime is a single process that builds one engine from one config, nl2sql.yaml, checks it, and invokes the pipeline per request.

docs.title: Runtime process layout
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Config[nl2sql.yaml and its files] --> App[Service Process]
    App --> Engine[NL2SQL engine]
    Engine --> Registries[Registries + Stores]
    Engine --> Graph[LangGraph Pipeline]
    Graph --> Exec[Executor Services]
    Exec --> DB[(Datasource)]

docs.title: Deployment inputs
docs.text:
• The config: nl2sql.yaml and the files it includes (nl2sql init writes them). The entry point finds it through NL2SQL_CONFIG, else ./nl2sql.yaml; the CLI also takes --config. See Configuration.
  • The environment: provider keys (OPENAI_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, OPENROUTER_API_KEY) and any variable the config names as ${env:VAR}. The CLI, nl2sql-api and the demo load the .env next to nl2sql.yaml at startup, never overriding a variable that is already set.
  • Adapter packages installed in the runtime environment.
  • A volume for storage.path: the vector index (index/), the state store (state.db: schema snapshots, the plan cache, feedback), run traces (traces/) and result files (results/).

docs.title: Startup
docs.text: Building the engine never connects. The entry points then call engine.check(): each datasource connects or is reported as failed and left out of routing, and each agent's key is checked without a model call. A datasource with required: true that cannot connect makes check() raise EngineNotReady, and the entry point refuses to start: nl2sql-api before it accepts a request, the CLI before it runs a command, nl2sql demo before it serves the playground.

docs.title: Runtime modes
docs.text:
• Local dev: nl2sql init, local embeddings, storage.path: .nl2sql.
  • Production: a mounted config, storage.path on a persistent volume, secrets from a secret provider, required: true on the datasources the service cannot run without, an observability exporter enabled.
  • Hosted demo: the playground on the shipped sample databases, holding no API key of its own; each visitor brings theirs. See Hosted demo.

docs.title: Scaling and isolation
docs.text:
• Orchestration runs in-process and can scale horizontally with your service.
  • There is no process-level sandbox. The graph runs on a one-worker thread pool inside your service process, so a driver-level crash takes the process down. If you need blast-radius containment, isolate at the deployment boundary — a replica or container you are willing to lose — and let your supervisor restart it. See ../execution/isolation.md.

docs.title: Source references
docs.text:
• The engine and its lifecycle: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/public_api.py
  • Building the runtime from the config: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/runtime.py
  • The config models and load_config: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/config/

docs.title: Docker Deployment
docs.text:
NL2SQL can be deployed as a standalone HTTP service using the nl2sql-api package and Docker. You can also embed the core library in your own service.

For the playground served as a public demo of the sample databases, where each visitor brings their own API key, see Hosted demo.

docs.title: Container requirements
docs.text:
• Install nl2sql-engine and add adapters via extras (e.g. nl2sql-engine[postgres]).
  • Provide the config: nl2sql.yaml and the files it includes, at the path NL2SQL_CONFIG names. packages/api/Dockerfile sets NL2SQL_CONFIG=/etc/nl2sql/nl2sql.yaml, so mount a config folder there.
  • Provide the provider keys and any variable the config reads as ${env:VAR}, in the environment or in a .env next to nl2sql.yaml (loaded at startup, never overriding a variable already set).

docs.title: Persistence mounts
docs.text:
Everything the engine writes lives under storage.path: the vector index (index/), the state store (state.db: schema snapshots, the plan cache and feedback), run traces (traces/) and result files (results/). Mount one volume and point storage.path at it, typically from the environment:

# storage.yaml
path: "${env:NL2SQL_DATA_DIR}"

docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 \
  -v "$PWD/config:/etc/nl2sql:ro" \
  -v nl2sql-data:/data -e NL2SQL_DATA_DIR=/data \
  -e OPENAI_API_KEY \
  nl2sql-api

See Storage.

docs.title: Startup
docs.text: The API builds the engine from the config and calls engine.check() before it accepts a request. A datasource with required: true that cannot connect stops the container (EngineNotReady in the log); any other one that fails is logged and left out of routing. Mark the datasources the service cannot run without required: true, so the orchestrator restarts a container that started broken.

docs.title: API roles
docs.text: nl2sql-api does not authenticate callers. Its api section says where the RBAC role comes from (api.role_header, a header an authenticating proxy sets, or a static api.role), and policies.admin_roles (default [admin]) says which roles may change datasources, LLMs and the index. With no role source, queries answer HTTP 401 and the admin routes answer HTTP 403, because a request through a published port does not come from loopback. See API settings, Caller role and Admin routes.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Schema indexing is not automatic; you must run indexing in your operational flow: nl2sql --config /etc/nl2sql/nl2sql.yaml index against the same storage, or POST /api/v1/index-all (admin role).
  • Observability exporters require network access; set settings.observability in the config.

docs.title: Reference configuration
docs.text: See Configuration for the whole config and the environment variables it reads.

docs.title: Hosted demo
docs.text:
nl2sql demo --hosted serves the playground as a public demo of the sample databases, where the server holds no API key and every visitor brings their own.

It is a third state, not a loosened --allow-settings. Locally, nl2sql demo saves your key to the demo project's .env and spends it on your questions; that is right on your own machine and wrong on a shared address. Hosted mode removes the key from the server entirely instead of relaxing the gate that protects it.

local (nl2sql demo) hosted (nl2sql demo --hosted) the API keys saved to the project's .env, used by the process one per provider, held by the browser tab, sent per request, used in memory, dropped a model per step written to the project's llm.yaml chosen in the browser tab, sent per request, saved nowhere Settings writes .env and llm.yaml writes nothing; the page keeps the keys and the choices Rebuild on (loopback, or --allow-settings) refused Answer ratings on (loopback, or --allow-settings) off Retrieval inspector on (loopback, or --allow-settings) on, read only, at the hosted rate Pipeline page on on, read only: it names the steps and their models, never a key --record supported refused before the server starts a visitor with no key replay mode, if no key is configured the guided questions replay recorded runs; anything else asks for a key the sample databases read-only read-only limits none a rate limit per visitor and a cap per session 
nl2sql demo --hosted --host 0.0.0.0 --port 7860 --questions-per-minute 6 --questions-per-session 30

There is no environment variable for it: hosted mode and its limits are flags on the command, and the container's CMD passes them.

docs.title: Recorded answers without a key
docs.text:
A visitor does not need a key to see the demo work. The guided questions are answered from recordings of real runs: every model step's actual reply to each guided question, captured once from a Claude model and shipped in the wheel at nl2sql/cli/demo/recordings/chinook.json (none ship until the first recording run below has been made and merged). At start-up the hosted server loads them into a replay server on loopback (the same FakeLLMServer local replay mode uses) and, for a question that carries no key:

  • a guided question with a recording runs the whole pipeline -- retrieval, the checks, SQL generation and the query against the sample database are all real and run now -- with each model step answered from the recording. The response carries "recorded": true, and the page puts a Recorded run badge beside the question, so nobody mistakes it for a live run. It is paced by the per-minute limit but not counted against the session cap, since it spends nothing.
  • anything else never runs. It answers 200 with "replay_miss": true and the sentence "No recorded answer for this question. Add an API key to ask it live."; the page shows that with an Add a key in Settings button.

With a key, every question -- guided or not -- runs live on that key, exactly as before. /api/meta lists the questions that replay as recorded, and the page marks those chips with a dot.

The model a replayed run names is the one that recorded it. The recordings file says which provider and model answered ({"provider": "anthropic", "model": "claude-opus-5", "recordings": [...]}; a bare list, the older format, still loads and names none). The hosted server's own config falls back to an OpenAI default, so without this a keyless visitor would be told a model produced the answer that did not. Instead, a keyless replay asks the replay server for the recorded model, which echoes it, so every call in the run's usage ledger -- and the Debug pane and the trace with it -- names claude-opus-5. /api/meta and /api/pipeline report the same recorded_with, and the Pipeline page shows that model on each model step, tagged recorded, until the visitor adds a key; then it shows the models their run will use, as before. Local replay mode (nl2sql demo with no key) does the same.

Verified answers replay too. The image's demo project has the six verified queries of its curated.yaml indexed (see Curated answers), so every question first asks the curated matcher's model call, VerifiedQueryChoice. The shipped recordings hold that call for every guided question, so a guided question a verified query answers replays with the Verified badge, and the rest replay the model's none_of_these and their generated answer. If a recording ever lacks the call, the matcher falls back (model_failed) and the run goes on to the recorded generated answer.

If no recordings ship (the file is missing or covers no guided question), the keyless path still works: the chips and the question box stay open and every question answers with the key prompt. The console line at start-up says which: "N guided questions answer from recordings without a key", or "No recordings ship with this install".

docs.title: Making the recordings
docs.text:
The recordings are made with a real Claude model, which costs money, so it is a deliberate act, never part of CI. Either:

  • Locally, from the repository root:
python scripts/record_demo_answers.py

It reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment or, failing that, from the repository root's .env (read with python-dotenv, never loaded into the environment; nothing prints the key), builds a fresh demo project, and runs nl2sql demo --record with that key passed as --api-key would pass it, so an exported OpenAI or OpenRouter key never wins. The script writes nothing to the environment. The demo records through the recording proxy on Anthropic's own wire with the Anthropic preset's default model, and writes packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/cli/demo/recordings/chinook.json, stamped with the provider and the model the proxy saw requested. A question is recorded only when its run succeeded -- rows, an answer, no error. A failed run's recordings are dropped, because every model call is recorded as it passes through the proxy and a run that failed in the aggregator would otherwise still count (a real run once said "Recorded 20 of 20" with ten failed). The file is written with the runs that succeeded, and every question that was not recorded is listed with its error. It exits 0 when every guided question was recorded, 1 when some were not or when the demo stopped before recording (its indexing failed: nl2sql demo --record refuses to record answers given against no index, and nothing is written), 2 with no key or without langchain-anthropic (pip install "nl2sql-engine[anthropic]"). Its output is safe to redirect to a file on Windows: it makes stdout and stderr UTF-8 before the demo prints anything. Review the diff and commit it. - In CI, Actions → Record demo answers → Run workflow (.github/workflows/record_demo.yml). It runs the same script with the repository secret ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and opens a pull request with the new recordings. It only ever runs by hand. The same workflow with record: clips re-records the playground home page's clips, which needs no key: Ask's clip is made from these recordings, so record the answers first.

The recordings ship inside the nl2sql-engine wheel, and the public Space runs released versions only, so merged recordings reach the Space with the next release (see Deployed by the release), not when their pull request merges.

tests/e2e/test_record_demo_answers_fake_llm.py runs the whole chain -- the script, the proxy on the Anthropic wire, a keyless hosted visitor replaying the result -- against a stand-in provider, so it is tested with no key and nothing spent.

docs.title: What the visitor's key does, and does not do
docs.text:
A visitor without a key is told what they can do before they ask. The Ask page opens with the pitch and, when recordings ship, the guided questions straight under it, the recorded ones marked; the key form (a provider choice, the key and Use this key, under three facts -- Stored in this browser tab only, Sent with each question in a request header, Never written to disk, logs or traces) is folded under Use your own key, and open from the start when nothing is recorded. Nothing is disabled: a question nobody recorded comes back with the way to add a key. The moment a key is saved the block clears, with no reload. The status pill in the top bar reads Hosted demo · Recorded runs (or Hosted demo · No key yet with nothing recorded), and once there is a key it names whose key answers (Hosted demo · OpenAI key in this tab), with the limits in its tooltip. None of this appears in local mode.

The visitor pastes a key on the Settings page, one per provider. From there:

  1. The browser keeps it, in that tab's sessionStorage, under that provider's own name. Closing the tab clears it. Nothing else in the page reads it.
  2. It travels as a request header of its own, X-NL2SQL-Api-Key-<provider> (X-NL2SQL-Api-Key-anthropic), on POST /api/ask (or its streamed twin, POST /api/ask/stream, which applies the same rules) and nowhere else. A header rather than the body, because a body is what request logs and validation errors quote back; one header per provider, so a key never shares a header with anything else and nothing that parses or quotes a header can expose two at once. With exactly one key the older X-NL2SQL-Api-Key is sent as well, and on its own it still means what it always did. The playground is served over plain HTTP locally and over the host's TLS when it is published, so deploy it behind HTTPS.
  3. The server uses it for that one request. It is bound to the request with nl2sql.llm.request_key and the LLM registry builds each step's client from it while the pipeline graph is constructed. The client is cached nowhere, so no later request and no other visitor can be handed it.
  4. Then it is gone. It is never written to a file, never put in an environment variable, never held in a module-level cache, and never included in a response.

A key sent without naming a provider has its provider read from its shape, exactly as --api-key does: sk-ant- is Anthropic, sk-or- is OpenRouter, anything else is OpenAI. Such a key also moves the model to that provider's default when it differs from the server's configured one, since a gpt- model means nothing to Anthropic.

docs.title: A model for each step
docs.text:
Choosing a model asks the server to remember nothing, so hosted mode keeps it. Under Model for each step on the Settings page (open beside the key card on a wide window, collapsed on a narrow one), the visitor can put each of the six model-using steps on a provider and model of their own. The choice lives in the same tab's sessionStorage and travels with each question in one more header:

X-NL2SQL-Models: {"astplanner":"anthropic:claude-opus-5"}

A compact JSON object, agent name to provider:model, and nothing else; it carries no secret, which is why it is the one header the server parses and the one thing a refusal repeats. A step with no entry runs on the configured default, so the simple path stays one key, the defaults, and a question.

The server checks every name against what the engine knows -- the pipeline's own steps, and the verified model lists in nl2sql/llm/providers.py -- before anything reaches a client. Each step is then built from the key for the provider it names: the planner can be on Claude while the answer writer stays on OpenAI, each calling its own endpoint with its own key.

A step whose chosen provider has no key is refused before the question runs, with 400 and a sentence naming both, for example "The Query planner step is set to run on Anthropic, but no Anthropic key was supplied. Add one under Settings, or put that step back on a provider you have a key for." Nothing is spent on the keys that were supplied. A step nobody chose a provider for is never refused this way: it takes the key for the provider it is configured on, or, failing that, the first key the request brought, exactly as a single key has always worked.

What it does not do:

  • It is not stored, so it cannot be reused for anyone else's question, and there is nothing to leak if the container is compromised later.
  • It does not reach a trace. Run traces are written as usual (that is what the playground's Debug drill-down reads), and the trace redactor is told about the request's key along with every other credential, so it is masked if it ever reaches a prompt or an error. The demo project's settings.yaml sets traces: { mode: always }, so every question leaves a file on the container's own disk; mode: on_failure keeps only the runs that went wrong.
  • It does not reach the log. Nothing logs the header, and errors about a key report its type, never its value.
  • It does not reach your data. The hosted demo answers only from the three sample databases shipped with the engine.

A question with no key at all is never a 401: it replays, or it is a replay miss that asks for a key (see above). A malformed key answers 400 without quoting what was sent, and no refusal ever repeats something shaped like a key, not even when one was pasted into the model header by hand.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
Both live in this one process's memory. There are no accounts, no analytics and no storage.

Limit Default Set by Keyed by Questions per minute 6 --questions-per-minute client address (a token bucket) Questions per session 30 --questions-per-session a random session cookie Query timeout 300s settings.pipeline.timeout_s in the demo's settings.yaml the run Rows returned 10,000 the demo datasources' limits.row_limit, bounded by settings.results.row_limit the query

Hitting one is a 429 with a sentence, never a stack trace: the rate limit says to wait a moment, the session cap says to run the demo locally for no limit at all. The retrieval inspector spends from the same rate bucket (it costs no tokens, but it does embed text) and does not count against the session's questions.

A question is charged when it arrives, before it runs, so one the visitor stops still counts toward both limits. Stopping does end the work: the page aborts its request, the server sees the connection close and cancels the run before its next step or model call (the call already in flight finishes).

The session cookie is a random token this process made up. It names no visitor, carries no key, and exists only so the session cap has something to count. A visitor who clears their cookies starts a new session; the rate limit, which is keyed by address, is what holds the pace down in the meantime.

docs.title: What is off, and what is on
docs.text:
Off: Settings persistence (choosing a model is on; it is only the saving that is off), Rebuild, answer ratings, and --record (refused before the server starts). --api-key is refused too: a server-side key is the one thing hosted mode is built to avoid, and any provider key exported into the process is cleared at start-up so nothing can fall back to it.

Rebuild being off is said on the page rather than left as a gap: the index panel reports that the index was built before the demo started and which databases it covers, and where the button would be it prints the server's own reason -- rebuilding writes to disk and the sample data never changes.

On: the guided questions without a key, from recorded runs; asking them or any other question live with a key; a key per provider and a model per step (both kept by the browser), the schema view of any of the three databases (the rail's Showing switcher), which database answered a run, the per-node Debug drill-down with its traces, and the retrieval inspector read-only.

docs.title: Read-only sample data
docs.text: The demo's three SQLite databases are configured with read_only: true under their connection options, which opens them through SQLite's own URI form with mode=ro. The driver refuses a write before any SQL is parsed, under the RBAC policy and the validator rather than instead of them. This is not specific to hosted mode: nothing in the engine writes to a demo database, so they are opened read-only everywhere.

docs.title: The container
docs.text:
deploy/huggingface/Dockerfile builds the playground as a hosted demo. It is a Space root rather than a repository build: it needs no build context, so the whole deploy is that one folder, copied to the Space's root.

It installs whatever the one build argument NL2SQL_SPEC names. On the Space that is always a released version from PyPI, nl2sql-engine[demo]==X.Y.Z, written into the copy of the Dockerfile the release pushes. The checked-in default is a GitHub archive of the tip of main, which is only what a local docker build gets; pass --build-arg NL2SQL_SPEC="nl2sql-engine[demo]==X.Y.Z" to build a release locally. Then it runs nl2sql init --demo /home/demo/demo and nl2sql index at build time, with NL2SQL_CONFIG=/home/demo/demo/nl2sql.yaml set in the image so every command and the server read that config. That bakes three things into the image so the container reaches nothing but the model at run time and the first question is answered at once:

  • the three sample databases and their config,
  • their vector index, built with the local embedder,
  • the local embedding model itself, roughly 79 MB of ONNX all-MiniLM-L6-v2 that chromadb would otherwise download on the first question. The 83 MB archive it was extracted from is deleted; chroma reaches for it only when the extracted files are missing.

The container runs as uid 1000 (not root), listens on $PORT (7860 by default, which is what a Space routes to), and carries a healthcheck that polls /api/health. That route reads nothing but process state and answers {"status": "ok", "version": "X.Y.Z"}, the installed nl2sql-engine version, in every mode; the release pipeline polls it on the live Space to know the new version is the one being served. Its CMD runs nl2sql demo --hosted --questions-per-minute 6 --questions-per-session 30; a public demo must never be started without --hosted.

cd deploy/huggingface
docker build -t nl2sql-demo .
docker run --rm -p 7860:7860 nl2sql-demo

docker compose up --build in the same folder does it through docker-compose.yml, which builds the same image with the same settings.

Measured on a build of this Dockerfile: 1175 MB on the container's own filesystem (docker image ls reports 1.65 GB, which includes the build attestations). Most of it is chromadb's transitive dependencies (polars, pyarrow, kubernetes, onnxruntime), which the vector store needs. Boot is about 5 seconds from docker run to the first answered request, and a guided question through a stand-in provider answered in 1.2 seconds.

docs.title: Deploying it as a Hugging Face Space
docs.text:
The Space is nadeem4nk/nl2sql-demo: public, Docker SDK, CPU basic. The full steps, and what each Space setting does, are in deploy/huggingface/README.md -- that file is also the Space's own front page, since a Docker Space reads its configuration from the front-matter of the README.md at its root.

The Space's public address is https://nl2sql.codewithnk.com, its custom domain; https://nadeem4nk-nl2sql-demo.hf.space serves the same app too. Both hosts serve every path, so deep links and API calls work on either:

curl https://nl2sql.codewithnk.com/api/health

The custom domain is set up in two places, and redoing it is the same two steps:

  1. On the Space: Settings -> Custom domain, enter nl2sql.codewithnk.com.
  2. At the DNS host for codewithnk.com: a CNAME record from nl2sql to hf.space.

Hugging Face checks the record and issues the TLS certificate itself; there is nothing to upload. Until it has, the domain fails with a certificate error and the hf.space address keeps working.

Never give the Space an API key, as a secret or otherwise. Hosted mode refuses to start when a provider key variable (OPENAI_API_KEY, OPENROUTER_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY) is set, because a key there would be spent by every visitor.

docs.title: Deployed by the release
docs.text:
The public Space runs released versions only, and a release deploys it with nothing to do by hand. Merging the release pull request tags vX.Y.Z, and publish_pypi.yaml then runs, in order:

flowchart LR
    PY[pypi: the three packages<br/>reach PyPI] --> PS[pypi-smoke: install X.Y.Z<br/>from PyPI, boot the demo]
    PS --> SP[space: publish_space.yml<br/>pins and pushes the Space]
    SP --> SS[space-smoke: the live URL<br/>reports X.Y.Z]
  1. pypi-smoke installs nl2sql-engine[demo]==X.Y.Z from PyPI into an empty virtualenv on a fresh runner, boots this same nl2sql demo --hosted with no key and checks it serves. The Space is never built on a version that does not install from PyPI.
  2. space calls publish_space.yml with the tag. It mirrors deploy/huggingface/ onto the Space's root, pins the image to the release, pushes, and waits for the Hub to build it. Before pushing it waits until PyPI's simple index lists X.Y.Z, and the Dockerfile retries its install (10 attempts, 30 seconds apart): the index the Hub's builder sees can lag a fresh upload, which is what failed v0.2.0's first Space build.
  3. space-smoke polls https://nadeem4nk-nl2sql-demo.hf.space/api/health until it reports X.Y.Z, then checks the page and /api/meta. A Space goes on serving its previous image while the new one builds, so a build that finished is not yet proof that visitors see it. It then runs the same check against the custom domain, SPACE_CUSTOM_DOMAIN at the top of publish_pypi.yaml, which proves the DNS record and certificate still reach the release; a fork sets its own domain there, or empties it to skip the check.

The whole release flow is in Releasing.

A push to main does not deploy the Space. It used to: every merge that touched the engine, the playground or this folder rebuilt the public demo from that commit, so the demo ran code no release contained, and a broken merge reached visitors before anyone had decided to ship it. Now a merge reaches the Space with the next release. Nothing is lost by waiting: the fresh-install job on every pull request builds the wheels, installs them as a user would and boots this exact command, so a change that would break the Space fails its PR. To see a change running on a Space before it is released, deploy it to a scratch Space of your own (below), never to the public one.

What a deploy puts at the Space root. The four files of deploy/huggingface/ -- Dockerfile, README.md (the Space's configuration and front page), docker-compose.yml, and SOURCE_SHA -- with two of them rewritten:

At the Space root What the deploy writes Dockerfile its ARG NL2SQL_SPEC= line: nl2sql-engine[demo]==X.Y.Z for a release, or a GitHub archive of the commit for a tagless run by hand SOURCE_SHA the full sha of the repository commit the deploy came from -- the tagged commit, on a release

The Dockerfile rewrite is what makes the Space run the release: the same bytes a user gets from pip install, not whatever main was at build time. Because the text of the ARG line changes with every release, the Hub always has a new commit to rebuild on and the layer cache below it is busted, so the engine is genuinely reinstalled. The workflow rewrites the default rather than passing --build-arg, because a Space build takes no build arguments from us; a grep right after the rewrite fails the deploy if that line is ever renamed, instead of quietly shipping a Space that builds something else.

The one secret. A Hugging Face access token with write permission (https://huggingface.co/settings/tokens), added as the repository secret HF_TOKEN at https://github.com/nadeem4/nl2sql/settings/secrets/actions. That is the only credential the workflow uses. release_please.yml and publish_pypi.yaml hand it down with secrets: inherit, since a called workflow sees no secret it is not given. Without it -- on a fork, or before it is added -- the deploy logs a line saying so and finishes green, space-smoke is skipped, and the rest of the release is unaffected; it never fails for a missing secret.

The token is read into the job's environment and used in exactly two places: by huggingface_hub, which picks HF_TOKEN up from the environment on its own, and as the password in the git push URL. It is never echoed, never traced (no set -x), and never written to a file: the Space remote is passed to each git command rather than saved into .git/config.

What it reports. The job never calls a build that did not happen a success. If the push produced a commit, the workflow checks the Space's head is that commit, then waits for a build to actually start and finish; a Space that never starts one within five minutes fails the job rather than reporting the previous build's RUNNING. If there was nothing to push -- the same release deployed twice -- the Hub starts no build on its own, so the workflow asks it for a factory rebuild (restart_space(..., factory_reboot=True)) whenever the Space is not running, and on every run by hand unless factory_rebuild is unticked, then waits for that build the same way; the summary reads "Factory rebuild". Only a release re-run against a Space already running that deploy skips the rebuild, and its summary reads "No rebuild". The job succeeds only when the Space ends RUNNING: a redeploy of v0.2.0 once found the Space in BUILD_ERROR, pushed nothing and still went green, which is what this closes. One deploy runs at a time; a run overtaken by a newer one is cancelled.

By hand. Actions → Publish Space → Run workflow, or:

$ gh workflow run publish_space.yml -f tag=v0.2.0

Four optional inputs: tag, the release to deploy; space_id, which defaults to nadeem4nk/nl2sql-demo; token_secret, the name of the secret holding the token, which defaults to HF_TOKEN; and factory_rebuild, on by default, which rebuilds the Space from scratch when there is nothing new to push. With a tag it does exactly what a release does. With no tag it deploys the commit of the branch it was run from, installed from a GitHub archive of that commit -- which is how to try an unreleased change on a Space: point space_id at a scratch Space of your own. Do not run it tagless against the public demo; that is the "unreleased code in public" this design exists to prevent.

What the first run does. The Space does not have to exist. The workflow calls create_repo(repo_type="space", space_sdk="docker", private=False, exist_ok=True), which makes a public Docker Space on CPU basic, then pushes the folder into it. On every later run exist_ok makes that call a no-op: the Hub ignores visibility, SDK and hardware for a Space that already exists, so a hardware upgrade or a visibility change made in the Space's own settings survives a deploy.

Rolling back. Run it by hand with the earlier tag, gh workflow run publish_space.yml -f tag=v0.1.9. It checks that tag out, pins the image to that version on PyPI and rebuilds, so the engine and the playground both go back. PyPI keeps every version, so any earlier release can be redeployed this way.

The workflow adds a commit on top of whatever the Space's main already is, so the Space's history is never rewritten and never lost -- including commits made in the Hub's own web editor. If a concurrent push lands between the workflow's fetch and its push, the push is refused and the job fails; re-running it picks up the new head and reapplies the folder. Nothing in the workflow force-pushes.

docs.title: By hand, as a fallback
docs.text:
If the workflow is unavailable, the owner can do the same thing from a clone:

  1. Create the Space at https://huggingface.co/new-space under nadeem4nk, named nl2sql-demo, SDK Docker (blank), CPU basic, public.
  2. Add it as a git remote: git remote add space https://huggingface.co/spaces/nadeem4nk/nl2sql-demo (pushing needs a write token from https://huggingface.co/settings/tokens).
  3. Push the folder as the Space root: git subtree push --prefix deploy/huggingface space main.

If step 3 is refused because the Space has commits of its own, git push space $(git subtree split --prefix deploy/huggingface main):main --force replaces the Space's history with this folder's. The workflow above never needs that, which is why it exists.

docs.title: The link preview
docs.text:
Two different links go around, and each unfurls from a different place:

Pasted link The card comes from https://nl2sql.codewithnk.com or https://nadeem4nk-nl2sql-demo.hf.space the Open Graph and Twitter tags in the page the app serves https://huggingface.co/spaces/nadeem4nk/nl2sql-demo short_description and thumbnail in deploy/huggingface/README.md's front-matter

Both show the same 1200x630 card:

The app's tags are added to the built page's <head> by preview.py as each request goes out, not baked into the bundle. A crawler runs no JavaScript, so a tag React adds on mount is a tag nobody sees; and og:image and og:url have to be absolute, while the same page is the Space, a container and http://127.0.0.1:8000. So the host comes off the request: X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-Host when a proxy set them (which is what the Space does), the Host header otherwise, and the URL the app itself saw if neither is a host. On the public Space, reached on either host, og:url, og:image and twitter:image all name https://nl2sql.codewithnk.com instead, so a shared link carries the short address. The card is served by the app at /social-card.png and ships in the wheel, so a pip install serves it too.

The Space's card reads thumbnail over raw GitHub rather than from the Space, so it works before the Space has built and while it is asleep.

docs.title: Regenerating the card
docs.text:
The card is rendered from scripts/social_card.html, which uses the playground's own colours and both of its typefaces. Edit that file, then:

cd web/playground && npm ci && cd ../..   # the fonts the card borrows
python scripts/render_social_card.py

Headless Chrome shoots it at 1200x630 and the script writes the same bytes to both places that need them: docs/assets/social-card.png, which the Space's thumbnail reads, and packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/cli/demo/playground/assets/social-card.png, which the app serves. A test holds the two byte-identical, so regenerating into only one of them fails rather than going out half-changed.

A card validator needs a public URL, so the check that the card really unfurls can only be run against the deployed Space, with X's card validator or https://opengraph.dev. What the tests check is everything up to that: the tags are in the served HTML, their URLs are absolute, and the image is served as image/png.

docs.title: The mark
docs.text: The wordmark's icon on the card is the playground's favicon, the plan spine: a root bar and stem with two indented steps, the typed plan the model writes, in outline. Its one copy is docs/assets/favicon.svg; the playground inlines it, this site uses it as its favicon, and the card redraws it in the light colours. See the playground README for where each copy lives.

docs.title: Running it locally instead
docs.text:
Hosted mode exists to show the engine on our sample data. To ask questions of your own data, with no limits and a key that never leaves your machine:

pip install "nl2sql-engine[demo]"
nl2sql demo

See Demo.

docs.title: Kubernetes Deployment
docs.text: Kubernetes deployment depends on the service you build around the engine, or on nl2sql-api. The engine expects one config, nl2sql.yaml, and the variables it names to be available to the runtime container.

docs.title: Configuration and secrets
docs.text:
Mount the config folder (a ConfigMap of nl2sql.yaml and the files it includes) and inject secrets so that:

  • NL2SQL_CONFIG names the mounted nl2sql.yaml (the API image defaults to /etc/nl2sql/nl2sql.yaml);
  • provider keys (e.g., OPENAI_API_KEY) and every variable the config reads as ${env:VAR} (database passwords, NL2SQL_DATA_DIR) are injected into env, or a secret provider in the secrets section reaches them.

Keys never go in the ConfigMap: the config holds references (password: "${env:SALES_DB_PASSWORD}"), not values.

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text: Everything the engine writes lives under storage.path: the vector index (index/), the state store (state.db), run traces (traces/) and result files (results/). Mount one persistent volume and point storage.path at it (path: "${env:NL2SQL_DATA_DIR}"). See Storage.

docs.title: Operational considerations
docs.text:
• Run schema indexing as a separate job or init container: nl2sql --config /etc/nl2sql/nl2sql.yaml index, on the same volume.
  • The API calls engine.check() before it serves. A datasource with required: true that cannot connect stops the pod, so a readiness gate on the process is enough; any other datasource that fails is logged and left out.
  • If you run nl2sql-api, set the role source in the api section (api.role_header behind an authenticating ingress, or api.role) and the admin roles (policies.admin_roles, default [admin]): pod traffic is not loopback, so without them the admin routes answer HTTP 403. See Admin routes.
  • Configure observability exporters in settings.observability (exporter, otlp_endpoint).

docs.title: Reference configuration
docs.text: See Configuration for the whole config and the environment variables it reads.

docs.title: Development Guide
docs.text: This guide focuses on extension points: adapters, executors, subgraphs, chunking, and planner logic.

docs.title: Extension guides
docs.text:
• extensions/add-adapter.md for new datasource adapters.
  • extensions/add-chunk-types.md for new schema chunk types.
  • extensions/extend-planner.md for planner/AST updates.
  • extensions/add-execution-backend.md for new executor services.

docs.title: The registry
docs.text:
Adapters, LLM providers, embeddings providers and secret providers are all found by name through nl2sql.registry.Registry (design). Each kind has an entry point group, and the built-ins are declared in packages/nl2sql/pyproject.toml in the same groups a plugin uses:

Kind Entry point group Interface Built-ins adapter nl2sql.adapters nl2sql_sdk.DatasourceAdapterProtocol sqlite, postgres, mysql, mssql, duckdb llm nl2sql.llms nl2sql.llm.providers.LLMProvider openai, anthropic, openrouter, ollama, made from PROVIDER_PRESETS embeddings nl2sql.embeddings nl2sql.embeddings.EmbeddingsProvider local, openai secrets nl2sql.secrets nl2sql_sdk.SecretProvider env, aws, azure, hashicorp
  • Registry.default() lists the installed entry points by name and imports none of them. Registry.empty() holds nothing.
  • add_adapter, add_llm, add_embeddings and add_secrets, and the decorators @registry.adapter(name) and so on, register in code on that registry only. A name already present raises unless replace=True.
  • names(kind) lists the names; load(kind, name) imports one and checks its interface_version, finds its driver_modules (adapters) or requires (LLM and embeddings providers) without importing them, and reports a name two installed packages declare. A failure is a RegistryError that says how to fix it, and an unknown name suggests the closest one.

After editing an entry point in pyproject.toml, reinstall the package (pip install -e packages/nl2sql): entry points are read from the installed metadata, not from the source tree.

docs.title: Subgraph extension overview
docs.text:
1. Implement a build_*_graph(ctx) function that returns a LangGraph runnable.
  2. Add it as a node in build_graph() and extend resolve_subgraph() with the capabilities the datasource must declare for it.
flowchart TD
    Subgraph[build_*_graph] --> Graph[build_graph]
    Graph --> Resolve[resolve_subgraph]
    Resolve --> Router[build_scan_layer_router]

docs.title: CLI console output
docs.text:
rich parses every string handed to Console.print, a Panel body, a Tree label or a table cell as console markup. Text the CLI did not author — exception messages, tracebacks, generated SQL, database errors, filesystem paths, LLM output, query result rows — must therefore never reach those APIs unescaped:

  • A closing-tag-shaped sequence ([/{style}], which appears in rich's own source and so in tracebacks through it) raises MarkupError and hides the real error.
  • A lowercase opening tag is consumed silently. T-SQL bracket-quoted identifiers are the common case: SELECT * FROM [dbo].[orders] renders as SELECT * FROM . unless the SQL is escaped.

Two conventions cover this:

  • Interpolating external text into a markup string: wrap it in rich.markup.escape, so the CLI's own styling still applies.
  • Passing external text as a whole cell, label or panel body: wrap it in rich.text.Text, which is never parsed as markup. ConsolePresenter.print_sql does this for plain strings; callers wanting styling pass a Text themselves.

Tracebacks are printed with console.print(..., markup=False).

docs.title: Source references
docs.text:
• Registry: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/registry.py
  • Subgraph selection: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/graph_utils.py
  • Adapter protocol: packages/sdk/src/nl2sql_sdk/protocols.py
  • SQL executor: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/execution/executor/sql_executor.py

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text:
The monorepo publishes three distributions to PyPI under unified versioning: they all carry the same version and are released together. Internal dependencies use compatible-release constraints (~=0.1), so a release only resolves for users if every package declares the same version.

Releases are automated. Nobody edits a version number and nobody edits CHANGELOG.md by hand — release-please owns both. Two steps are manual. First, the release page docs/releases/X.Y.Z.md is written with the release-notes skill and merged. A status check on the release PR stays red until it is. Second, the owner merges the release pull request. Everything after that runs on its own: the three packages go to PyPI, the API image to GHCR, the versioned docs to gh-pages, and the hosted demo on Hugging Face is rebuilt on the version just published. Each of those is checked from the outside before the release counts as done.

docs.title: The automated flow
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    C[Conventional Commit merged to main] --> RP[release_please.yml]
    RP --> PR[Release PR: CHANGELOG.md + version bumps]
    PR --> RN[release-notes skill: docs/releases/X.Y.Z.md<br/>merged to main in its own PR]
    RN -->|release-notes status turns green| PR2[Release PR refreshed]
    PR2 -->|the owner merges it| TAG[Tag vX.Y.Z + GitHub Release]
    TAG --> NOTES[release-notes job: page summary<br/>above the generated changelog]
    TAG -->|release_please.yml calls it with tag_name<br/>the tag itself cannot trigger it| B[publish_pypi.yaml: build 3 dists]
    B --> S{wheels install and import?}
    S -->|no| STOP[Nothing is published]
    S -->|yes| PY[PyPI via trusted publishing:<br/>one job per package,<br/>one environment each]
    PY --> GH[ghcr.io/nadeem4/nl2sql-api]
    PY --> D[mike deploy: versioned docs]
    PY --> PS[pypi-smoke: pip install the release<br/>from PyPI, boot the demo]
    PS --> SP[publish_space.yml: Space pinned to<br/>nl2sql-engine demo == X.Y.Z]
    SP --> SS[space-smoke: the live Space<br/>reports version X.Y.Z]

The same chain runs on every pull request up to the point of publishing: the build and fresh-install jobs in test.yml build the wheels, install them the way a user does and boot the demo, and the api-image job builds the GHCR image from packages/api/Dockerfile (without pushing it), so a release does not meet these checks for the first time.

docs.title: 1. Commit messages decide the version
docs.text:
The bump comes from Conventional Commits on main, so the commit subject is the release input:

Commit prefix Effect on the next version fix: patch feat: minor any type with ! or a BREAKING CHANGE: footer major docs:, perf:, deps:, revert: patch, and shown in the changelog refactor: no release on its own, shown in the changelog chore:, ci:, test:, build:, style: no release on their own, hidden from the changelog

Which types reach the changelog is set by changelog-sections in release-please-config.json. Miscellaneous Chores (chore:) is hidden there, and so are ci:, test:, build: and style:. A breaking change is shown whatever its type. A chore: commit carrying a Release-As: footer has still shown up under Miscellaneous Chores (release 0.2.2). If that keeps happening, put the footer on a commit of a visible type.

The project is pre-1.0: a breaking change bumps the minor

release-please-config.json sets top-level bump-minor-pre-major: true, which the schema describes as "Breaking changes only bump semver minor if version < 1.0.0". While the version is below 1.0.0, a feat!: or a BREAKING CHANGE: footer therefore moves 0.1.0 to 0.2.0 rather than to 1.0.0 — semver's rule for an unstable public API.

Without this setting the first breaking commit silently declares the project stable. That is exactly what happened before it was added: the refactor!: that collapsed the distributions made release-please propose 1.0.0.

Going to 1.0.0 is then a deliberate act: set the version explicitly with a Release-As: 1.0.0 commit (below). The flag stays true afterwards and becomes a no-op once the version is >= 1.0.0.

docs.title: 2. release_please.yml maintains a release PR
docs.text:
Every push to main runs googleapis/release-please-action@v4. It keeps a single open pull request (separate-pull-requests: false, one manifest entry for the whole repo) that contains the accumulated CHANGELOG.md entry and the version bump applied everywhere it appears:

File Updated by CHANGELOG.md the python release strategy pyproject.toml (repo root) the python release strategy packages/sdk/pyproject.toml an extra-files generic updater packages/nl2sql/pyproject.toml an extra-files generic updater packages/api/pyproject.toml an extra-files generic updater .release-please-manifest.json release-please

The three package manifests carry a marker comment on their version line:

version = "0.1.0" # x-release-please-version

The generic updater replaces the semver-looking value on any line carrying that annotation. The type: "generic" entry in release-please-config.json is required: without it a .toml path gets the TOML updater, which addresses a field by jsonpath and ignores the marker entirely. The comment is a plain TOML comment and has no effect on the build.

Because include-component-in-tag is false, the tag is vX.Y.Z rather than nl2sql-vX.Y.Z.

docs.title: 3. Every release needs a release page
docs.text:
Every version has a plain-language page at docs/releases/X.Y.Z.md, listed on the Releases page. The changelog lists commits. The page says what the release is for, what it does not do yet, and how to upgrade. It is written by the release-notes Claude Code skill (.claude/skills/release-notes/SKILL.md), which uses a fixed template (template.md next to it) and matches the last two pages. So every page has the same structure.

The order, once release-please has opened its PR:

  1. Run the release-notes skill. It reads the version from the release PR, gathers the commits, PRs and changelog section, writes docs/releases/X.Y.Z.md, adds it to docs/releases/index.md and the mkdocs.yml nav, runs mkdocs build --strict, and opens a PR titled docs(release): notes for X.Y.Z.
  2. Merge the notes PR to main. It cannot go on the release branch, because release-please rewrites that branch every time main changes.
  3. The gate goes green. The merge is a push to main, so release-please refreshes its PR, and the release-notes-gate job in release_please.yml checks again.
  4. The owner merges the release PR.

The gate is the release-notes commit status on the release PR's head commit. The release-notes-gate job sets it on every push to main that did not tag a release. It reads the version from the release branch's .release-please-manifest.json. Then it runs python scripts/release_notes.py check --version X.Y.Z against main. The check fails unless the page exists and has a summary block. While it fails, the status is red and its description says to run the release-notes skill.

Why a status from release_please.yml, not a pull_request check

release-please pushes its branch with GITHUB_TOKEN. GitHub opens pull_request runs for that push in the action_required state, and they never start unless someone approves each one. That is why test.yml has no runs on the release PRs. A job in release_please.yml runs on the same push that refreshes the PR, so the status always describes the PR's latest head. It needs no extra token: statuses: write on that job is enough.

The status blocks a merge only if it is required: add release-notes as a required status check in a branch ruleset for main. Until then it is a red mark that the owner reads before merging.

The page's first paragraph, between <!-- summary:start --> and <!-- summary:end -->, also goes into the GitHub Release. See the release-notes job below.

docs.title: 4. Merging the release PR is the gate
docs.text: This is the only manual step in a release, after the release page. Merging the pull request makes release-please create the vX.Y.Z tag and publish the GitHub Release. Until someone merges it, nothing is tagged and nothing is published. Reviewing the changelog and the version it proposes is the release decision.

docs.title: 5. The release publishes everything
docs.text:
publish_pypi.yaml runs a chain of seven jobs:
